title: Course Syllabus
text:
Course Description (Catalog Description)
Euclidean spaces, matrices and matrix arithmetic, solving systems of equations, and eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Emphasis on applications and use of computation.
Division: Lower Division.
Weekly: Lecture 3 hrs.
Instruction Mode: Face to face only.
Prerequisite: (MATH 101 and MATH 101T) or MATH 102 or ALEKS PPL assessment score 78–100 or appropriate high school coursework. All prerequisite courses must be passed with a grade of C− or higher. See Math Placement and ALEKS PPL for details.
Note: if you plan to use MATH 107 as a prerequisite for another MATH, DATA, or STAT course, you must have a grade of C− or better in this course.

Course Learning Outcomes
By the end of this course, students will be able to:

Interpret matrices, vectors, and complex numbers, both algebraically and geometrically.
Solve systems of linear equations using row-reduction techniques by hand and with software.
Find eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix by hand for a \(2\times 2\) matrix and with software for general cases.
Understand and apply eigenvalues and eigenvectors to solve problems.
Recognize special types of matrices and their properties, such as triangular, symmetric, and positive definite matrices.
Communicate in the language of linear algebra, including linear combination, subspace, span, independence, basis, and dimension.
Write or adapt programs to implement linear algebra concepts, such as matrix arithmetic, vectors, and plotting.
Apply linear algebra to real-world problems.
Learn independently as well as collaboratively. Develop study techniques that include pre- and post-reading of class materials and be able to critically analyze and implement solutions in a team setting.

Daily learning objectives for each meeting are on Lectures.


General Education & Institutional Learning Outcomes
This course fulfills Lower Division General Education Area 2 (Mathematics) and supports Cal Poly Humboldt’s Institutional Learning Outcomes related to quantitative reasoning, critical thinking, and communication.

Course Materials & Workload
MATH 107 includes three weekly lecture meetings. Some Fridays (and a few other days) include a lab, quiz, or exam as marked on the schedule.
In this 3-unit course, students should expect to spend approximately 9 hours per week on course-related work, including time in class (3 hours) and time outside of class on reading, practice, labs, and exam preparation (6 hours).

Required Materials
Course website: Canvas and https://roverhol.github.io/math107
Textbooks (free):

Stephen Boyd and Lieven Vandenberghe, Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra: Vectors, Matrices, and Least Squares (VMLS).
Gilbert Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra: selected free MIT samples only (§3.5, §6.1, and SVD slides), so you do not need to buy it.

Software: Octave or Python (pick one for the term). Lab hubs have both versions; see Resources and Lab 0.

Other Technology: A scientific calculator for in-class assessments and regular access to a computer with reliable internet. Bring a laptop on lab days, or let me know a day ahead that I should bring one for you to use. Please bring paper and a pen or pencil to class each day.


Access & Affordability
Students who do not have personal access to required technology may use computers either in campus labs or checked out from the library. Calculators are also available for check out from the library’s front desk. If you want to get a free used computer, please check to see if our campus’s Reusable Office Supply Exchange (ROSE) has one available.


Fees
There are no additional course fees beyond standard tuition and registration fees.

title: Course Syllabus
text:
Late or Missed Work Policies
The policies for late or missed work are as follows:

Lecture attendance is required, but I know that sometimes you will need to miss class due to illness or other emergencies. Each student may miss up to 10 lecture days without penalty and without contacting me. Reserve these days for emergencies. In my experience, it is rare for a student to succeed if they regularly miss class or are absent for more than two weeks, so if you find yourself in that situation, please communicate with me and your advisor so we can help you find a solution.
Quizzes are in the first 10 minutes of class. The lowest two quiz scores are dropped. If you must miss a quiz due to illness or another emergency, please contact me to arrange a makeup.
Labs are credited in class on the dates on the schedule: complete the hub exercises, handwrite the one-pager, and get initials. After a week, missed lab credit is not made up except by arrangement (e.g. illness).
Capstone work is due on the dates on the schedule. Late project work cannot be turned in due to the end of the semester and course grades being due. If you are unable to complete the project in time, you should consider whether your situation is such that an Incomplete grade is appropriate. This would give you more time to complete the course.
Midterms and the final exam are required. If you need to miss a midterm due to illness or another emergency, communicate with me as soon as possible to reschedule.

Note: Technology issues (internet access, device failure, software problems) are not automatically considered valid excuses for late or missed work; students are expected to plan accordingly.


AI Policy
Much of your course grade will be based on work you produce in class (quizzes and exams) without having the option of using AI as a resource.
Outside of in-class assessments, you may use AI, such as NotebookLM or ChatGPT, to help you learn the material or to get unstuck on labs or the capstone.
For work that you do at home that is turned in for a grade I have two requirements:

If you used AI, acknowledge this briefly in the document (you don’t need to state in detail how you used AI or give your prompts, just the name of the AI service you used).
Be responsible for the correctness and appropriateness of all (AI-assisted or not) materials you turn in.

I may use AI to assist me in my delivery of the course material, such as asking whether an assignment is appropriate for a college-level course or whether the wording of a quiz question could be improved. I will not use AI to grade your work or use an AI detection tool to check your work.

Indexing reminder: Boyd’s \(x_1\) is the first entry. Octave is 1-based (x(1)). Python / NumPy is 0-based (x[0]).

Vectors and basics








Task
Octave
Python (NumPy)

Add / scale
x+y, 2*x
x+y, 2*x


Dot product \(x^{\mathsf{T}}y\)
x'*y
x @ y or np.dot(x,y)


Plot in 2D
plot(x(1), x(2), 'o')
plt.scatter(x[0], x[1]) (after import matplotlib.pyplot as plt)





Norm, distance, angle








Task
Octave
Python (NumPy)




Norm \(\lVert x\rVert\)
norm(x)
np.linalg.norm(x)


Distance \(\lVert x-y\rVert\)
norm(x-y)
np.linalg.norm(x-y)


Cosine similarity
(a'*b)/(norm(a)*norm(b))
(a @ b)/(np.linalg.norm(a)*np.linalg.norm(b))


Angle (degrees)
acosd(cos_th)
np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(cos_th,-1,1)))





Many candidates (rows of a matrix)
Store each candidate as a row of Z. Query x is a column in Octave examples below (transpose with x' when subtracting from rows).








Task
Octave
Python (NumPy)




Stack candidates as rows
Z = [1 2; 3 4; 5 6]

All distances to x
d = sqrt(sum((Z - x').^2, 2))
d = np.linalg.norm(Z - x, axis=1)


Nearest index
[~, j] = min(d) → 1-based
j = np.argmin(d) → 0-based


Smallest distance
min(d)
np.min(d)





Matrices and \(Ax=b\)
b is a column. In Python, * is entrywise; matrix multiplication is @. Run import numpy as np first.

A @ x


Augmented \([A\mid b]\)
M = [A b]

Left-multiply by \(E\)
M = E * M
M = E @ M

Check \(Ax-b\)

title: Quiz 11
text:
Core

Fluency (complete prompts � practice these by hand)
C11.1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
v=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(Av\). Is \(v\) an eigenvector? If so, what is \(\lambda\)?
C11.2. You are told that \(v=(1,-1)\) is an eigenvector of \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{bmatrix}.
\] Find \(\lambda\) by comparing components of \(Av\) and \(v\). Then verify \(Av=\lambda v\).
C11.3. Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1.2,\,0.5)\) (Lab 4 / Lecture 35 long-run pattern).

Name two real eigenpairs using the standard basis.
If \(x_0=(1,1)\), write \(x_t=A^t x_0\) componentwise. Which term dominates for large \(t\)?

C11.4. Complex drill. Let \(z=2+i\) and \(w=1-3i\). Compute \(z+w\), \(zw\), and \(|z|\).
C11.5. For \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{bmatrix},
\] form \(\det(A-\lambda I)\), find both eigenvalues, and give one eigenvector for \(\lambda=3\).
C11.6. Rotation. Let \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (\(90^\circ\) CCW).

Show that the characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^2+1=0\), so \(\lambda=\pm i\).
Why does this match the geometric fact that \(R\) has no real eigenvector?

C11.7. Check a complex pair. With \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(v=(1,-i)\), compute \(Av\) and decide whether \(Av=iv\) or \(Av=(-i)v\).
C11.8. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(Av=2v\) and \(v\neq 0\), then \(A^3 v=8v\).
C11.9 (Lab 5 / software). Suppose Octave/Python reports eigenvalues of a \(2\times 2\) matrix as approximately \(0.9\) and \(0.2\), with corresponding eigenvectors \(v_1\approx(0.7,\,0.7)\) and \(v_2\approx(-0.7,\,0.7)\) (normalized). For dynamics \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) started near \(v_1+v_2\), which mode dominates for large \(t\), and does the state grow or decay?
C11.10 (Lab 5 / verify). Software prints \(\lambda\approx 3\) and \(v\approx(0.707,\,0.707)\) for \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.
\] Explain how you would verify \(Av\approx\lambda v\) numerically in one or two lines of code (Octave or Python). What should \(\|Av-\lambda v\|\) look like if the pair is correct?

L Ch. 5 Ex. 2: Markov equilibrium/eigenvector portions

title: Quiz 9
text:
Core

Fluency (complete prompts � practice these by hand)
C9.1. Let \(a=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\0\end{bmatrix}\), \(b=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{bmatrix}\), and \(c=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\\1\end{bmatrix}\).

Form the outer product \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) (give the \(3\times 3\) matrix).
Compute \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) and \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\). Confirm they are equal as vectors.

C9.2. In C9.1, which evaluation order stores a full \(3\times 3\) intermediate matrix? Which only needs a scalar intermediate \(b^{\mathsf{T}}c\)? In one sentence, why does the second order win for large \(n\) when \(a,b,c\in\mathbb{R}^n\)?
C9.3. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Interpret \(ABx\) as �apply \(B\), then \(A\).� Compute \(Bx\), then \(A(Bx)\). Also compute \(BAx\). Is \(AB=BA\)?
C9.4. Dimensions. For each pair, decide whether \(AB\) is defined and give the size of \(AB\) if it is.

\(A\) is \(4\times 2\), \(B\) is \(2\times 3\).
\(A\) is \(3\times 2\), \(B\) is \(3\times 2\).
\(A\) is \(2\times 2\), \(B\) is \(2\times 5\).

C9.5. Compute \[
\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\3&2\end{bmatrix}
\] by forming columns \(Ab_1\) and \(Ab_2\) (or by row�column inner products).
C9.6. Stage 1: \(B=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\). Stage 2: \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (\(90^\circ\) CCW). Write the single matrix \(M\) for �\(B\) then \(A\)� and compute \(M(1,1)\).
C9.7. Let \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (swap coordinates) and \(x_0=(4,1)\). Compute \(A^2\) and \(x_2=A^2 x_0\). Interpret \(A^2\) in one sentence.
C9.8. Directed graph on nodes \(\{1,2,3\}\) with adjacency (Boyd: \(A_{ij}=1\) means edge from \(j\) to \(i\)) \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 0 \\
1 & 1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Given \[
A^2=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix},
\] what does \((A^2)_{31}\) mean? How many length-\(2\) walks from node \(1\) to node \(3\)?
C9.9. For dynamics \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\), true or false with a one-line reason: \(x_5=A^5 x_0\) and also \(x_5=A x_4\).
C9.10 (cost). You need \(y=(ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) for tall vectors of length \(n=1000\). Roughly how many numbers are stored in the intermediate \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\)? Roughly how many in the scalar \(b^{\mathsf{T}}c\)? Which plan would you time in software, and why?

title: Quiz 7
text:
Core

Fluency (complete prompts — practice these by hand)
C7.1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(Ae_1\) and \(Ae_2\) for \(e_1=(1,0)\) and \(e_2=(0,1)\). In one sentence, how do those two images sit inside \(A\)?
C7.2. Reflection through the \(x_1\)-axis sends \(e_1=(1,0)\mapsto(1,0)\) and \(e_2=(0,1)\mapsto(0,-1)\). Write \(A\), compute \(A(2,3)\), and draw \(e_1\), \(e_2\), and both images on one set of axes.
C7.3. Rotation by \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise. Write the matrix. Where do \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) land? Draw those two arrows, then draw the unit square with vertices \((0,0)\), \((1,0)\), \((1,1)\), \((0,1)\) and its image.
C7.4. Stretch by \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1/2)\). Where do \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) land? Draw the same unit square and its image.
C7.5. Slant (shear) by \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Where do \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) land? Draw the unit square and its image. What shape is the image?
C7.6. Flip through the \(x_2\)-axis: build \(A\) by tracking \(e_1\) and \(e_2\). The triangle has vertices \((0,0)\), \((2,0)\), and \((1,1)\). Compute the three image points and draw the original triangle and the image.
C7.7. Let \(X=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}\) (columns are three vertices) and \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\). Compute \(AX\). Draw the original triangle and the image, and describe the effect in one sentence.
C7.8. The rectangle has vertices \((0,0)\), \((2,0)\), \((2,1)\), \((0,1)\). Apply the \(90^\circ\) counterclockwise rotation from C7.3 to each vertex. Draw the original rectangle and the image.
C7.9. Using the shear in C7.5, where does the single point \((0,2)\) land? You may use that \((0,2)=2e_2\). Draw the point and its image.

title: Lecture 40 — SVD and capstone launch
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Interpret \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}\) conceptually.
Construct a rank-\(k\) approximation computationally.
Compare singular-value decay for an image/frame and a frame-difference matrix.
Encode three frames either independently or as \(F_1\), \(D_2\), \(D_3\).
Compare reconstruction error and storage for the two approaches.
Formulate a capstone question involving accuracy, storage, runtime, and resource use.

(Objectives 3–6 are launched today and carried in the capstone packet.)

title: Lecture 40 — SVD and capstone launch
text:
Warm-up (after quiz)
A grayscale image (or one video frame) is an \(m\times n\) matrix of pixel intensities.

Roughly how many numbers store the full matrix?
If most “information” lived in a few patterns, why might a factored low-rank form save storage?

title: Lecture 40 — SVD and capstone launch
text:
Fill in
SVD (conceptual). Every real \(m\times n\) matrix factors as \[
A = U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}},
\] where the columns of \(U\) and \(V\) are orthonormal (left / right singular vectors) and \(\Sigma\) is rectangular “diagonal” with nonnegative singular values \[
\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge 0
\] on its main diagonal. Think: \(A\) = rotate/reflect → stretch by \(\sigma_i\) → rotate/reflect.
Rank-\(k\) approximation. Keep the largest \(k\) singular values (and matching singular-vector columns); set the rest to zero. The truncated product \[
A_k = U_k\Sigma_k V_k^{\mathsf{T}}
\] is the best rank-\(k\) approximation in the usual 2-norm / Frobenius sense (details in the slides / capstone).
Software sketch (capstone / later):








Task
Octave
Python




SVD
[U,S,V] = svd(A)
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)


Rank-\(k\) rebuild
use first \(k\) columns / \(\sigma\)’s
U[:,:k] @ np.diag(S[:k]) @ Vt[:k,:]



Capstone launch (one question). For a short clip of frames: when is it better to compress each frame alone versus encode \(F_1\) and differences \(D_2=F_2-F_1\), \(D_3=F_3-F_2\)? Trade off accuracy, storage, runtime, and resource use — including the cost of computing the SVD itself. Full prompts live in the capstone packet; studio is Mon Dec 7.

title: Lecture 40 — SVD and capstone launch
text:
Worked in class (short)
W1. Read \(\Sigma\). Suppose a \(4\times 3\) matrix has singular values \(\sigma=(10,\,2,\,0.1)\). What is \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\) (numerically “full” vs tiny)? For a rank-\(1\) approximation, which \(\sigma\) do you keep?
W2. Storage cartoon. Full \(m\times n\) needs \(mn\) entries. A rank-\(k\) factorization stores about \(k(m+n+1)\) numbers (columns of \(U_k\), \(V_k\), and \(k\) singular values). When is \(k(m+n+1)\ll mn\)?
W3. Frames vs differences (launch). Three frames \(F_1,F_2,F_3\). Plan A: compress each. Plan B: compress \(F_1\), \(D_2=F_2-F_1\), \(D_3=F_3-F_2\). In one sentence each: when might Plan B win on storage? What must you still check (error / runtime)?

title: Lecture 40 — SVD and capstone launch
text:
Your turn
Y1. In \(A=U\Sigma V^{\mathsf{T}}\), what do the singular values measure conceptually (one phrase)?
Y2. True or false: computing an SVD is always “free,” so low-rank multiplication is always faster overall.
Y3. Write one capstone question you care about (accuracy, storage, runtime, or resource use) for frames vs frame-differences. One sentence is enough — expand in studio.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Stretch factors / importance of each singular-vector mode (how strongly \(A\) amplifies that direction).
Y2. False. The factorization itself can be expensive; low-rank reuse only pays off when approximation quality is good and you reuse the factors enough (see capstone notes).
Y3. Any clear tradeoff question is fine — e.g. “For my three frames, does difference encoding cut storage at the same relative error, after counting SVD time?”

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Download PDF
Last updated: October 8, 2026.
Boyd video (optional): Lecture 33 — least squares · ENGR108 playlist (Boyd)
Textbook: Boyd & Vandenberghe, VMLS (PDF)
Reading: Boyd 12.1. Related objectives: Lectures. Schedule.
Bring paper. Warm-up while attendance is taken, then fill-in notes, board examples, and Your turn.
Look ahead: Wednesday fits data and checks positive definiteness; Friday’s quiz / lab / SVD launch are on the schedule.

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Recognize an inconsistent overdetermined system.
Formulate the least-squares objective \(\min_x \lVert Ax-b\rVert\).
Interpret the fitted vector as the closest attainable vector.
Interpret the residual geometrically.
Distinguish an exact solution from a best approximate solution.

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Warm-up
Consider the overdetermined system \(Ax=b\) with \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
b=\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{bmatrix}.
\]

How many equations? How many unknowns? Is \(A\) tall, wide, or square?
Suppose someone guesses \(x=(1,0.5)\). Compute \(Ax\) and \(Ax-b\). Is \(x\) an exact solution?

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Fill in
Overdetermined / inconsistent. When there are more independent equations than unknowns, \(Ax=b\) often has \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) exact solution. The right-hand side \(b\) may lie outside the column space \(C(A)\).
Least-squares idea. Instead of insisting on \(Ax=b\), choose \(\hat{x}\) to make \(A\hat{x}\) as close as possible to \(b\): \[
\hat{x}\;=\;\arg\min_x\;\lVert Ax-b\rVert.
\] The vector \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) attainable right-hand side in \(C(A)\).
Residual. The residual is \[
r = b - A\hat{x}
\] (some texts write \(A\hat{x}-b\); same length \(\|r\|\)). Geometrically, \(r\) is the leftover after projecting \(b\) onto \(C(A)\) — it is orthogonal to every column of \(A\) at a minimizer (Wednesday).
Exact vs approximate.







Situation
Meaning




Exact solution
\(Ax=b\) for some \(x\) \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(b\in\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\)


Least-squares solution
minimizes \(\|Ax-b\|\); residual may be \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)



If an exact solution exists, it is also a least-squares solution (residual zero).

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Worked in class
W1. Inconsistent check. For the warm-up \(A\) and \(b\), argue that no \(x=(x_1,x_2)\) can satisfy all three equations simultaneously. (Hint: equations 1–2 force \(x_2=1\); plug into equation 3.)
W2. Objective value. With the same \(A,b\) and trial \(x=(1,0.5)\), compute \(\|Ax-b\|\) (Euclidean). Is this the minimum? (You need not prove optimality yet — just evaluate the objective.)
W3. Closest attainable vector. Sketch (in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) as a cartoon, or think in words): \(C(A)\) is a plane (or line) through the origin; \(b\) is off the plane; \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) is the foot of the perpendicular from \(b\) to \(C(A)\). Label the residual \(r=b-\hat{b}\).
W4. Exact case. Change \(b\) to \(b'=(1,2,3)\). Show that \(x=(1,1)\) solves \(Ax=b'\) exactly. What is the residual? What is \(\min_x\|Ax-b'\|\)?
W5. Language check. In one sentence each, distinguish “no solution” from “best approximate solution.”

title: Lecture 38 — When \(Ax=b\) has no exact solution
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
b=\begin{bmatrix}3\\1\\1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x=\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(Ax\) and \(r=b-Ax\). Is \(x\) an exact solution? What is \(\|r\|\)?
Y2. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(Ax=b\) is inconsistent, then no vector \(\hat{x}\) can make \(\|A\hat{x}-b\|\) finite.
Y3. In words: what does \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\) represent when \(\hat{x}\) is a least-squares solution?
Y4. A \(4\times 2\) matrix \(A\) has linearly independent columns, and \(b\notin C(A)\). Can \(Ax=b\) have an exact solution? Can it have a least-squares solution?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(Ax=(2,1,1)\); \(r=(1,0,0)\); not exact. \(\|r\|=1\).
Y2. False. The residual norm is always finite; least squares still chooses an \(\hat{x}\) that minimizes it (even when the minimum is positive).
Y3. \(\hat{b}\) is the closest vector in the column space \(C(A)\) to the observed \(b\) — the attainable right-hand side under the model \(Ax\).
Y4. Exact: no (\(b\notin C(A)\)). Least squares: yes (minimizer of \(\|Ax-b\|\) still exists; uniqueness follows from independent columns).

title: Lecture 36 — Characteristic equation, \(2	imes 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Interpret \(a+bi\) algebraically and as a point/vector in the complex plane.
Perform the basic complex arithmetic needed for eigenvalue calculations.
Form and solve \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) for a \(2\times 2\) matrix.
Find corresponding eigenvectors.
Check real or complex eigenpairs by substitution.

title: Lecture 36 — Characteristic equation, \(2	imes 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers
text:
Warm-up
Monday’s rotation \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) had no real eigenvector.

Form \(R-\lambda I\) and compute \(\det(R-\lambda I)\) as a quadratic in \(\lambda\).
What are the roots? Are they real?

title: Lecture 36 — Characteristic equation, \(2	imes 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers
text:
Fill in
Complex numbers. A complex number is \(z=a+bi\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(i^2=\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\). Plot \(z\) as the point \((a,b)\) in the complex plane.
Arithmetic (what we need):

Add/subtract: combine real and imaginary parts.
Multiply: \((a+bi)(c+di)=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i\).
Conjugate: \(\overline{a+bi}=\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\).
Magnitude: \(|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\).

Characteristic equation. Eigenvalues of square \(A\) solve \[
\det(A-\lambda I)=0.
\] For \(2\times 2\), this is a \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) equation in \(\lambda\).
Eigenvectors. For each eigenvalue \(\lambda\), solve \[
(A-\lambda I)v=0,\qquad v\neq 0
\] (null space of \(A-\lambda I\)). Scale freely — any nonzero multiple is fine.
Check. Always verify \(Av=\lambda v\) by substitution (works for real or complex pairs).

title: Lecture 36 — Characteristic equation, \(2	imes 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers
text:
Worked in class
W1. Complex drill. Let \(z=2+i\) and \(w=1-3i\).

Compute \(z+w\), \(zw\), and \(\overline{z}\).
Plot \(z\) and \(\overline{z}\) in the complex plane.

W2. Real \(2\times 2\) by hand. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Expand \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) and solve for \(\lambda\).
For each eigenvalue, find one eigenvector.
Check one pair by computing \(Av\) and \(\lambda v\).

W3. Rotation eigenvalues. For \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\):

Confirm the characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^2+1=0\), so \(\lambda=\pm i\).
For \(\lambda=i\), solve \((R-iI)v=0\) and give one complex eigenvector.
Check \(Rv=iv\) by matrix–vector multiplication (complex arithmetic).

W4. Interpretation preview. Complex conjugate eigenvalues of a real matrix often signal \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) (rotation / oscillation) in the real plane — Friday’s lab makes this concrete with software.

title: Lecture 36 — Characteristic equation, \(2	imes 2\) eigenproblems, and complex numbers
text:
Your turn
Y1. Compute \((3-2i)(1+i)\) and \(|3-2i|\).
Y2. For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\), form \(\det(A-\lambda I)\), find both eigenvalues, and an eigenvector for \(\lambda=3\).
Y3. Check: with \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(v=(1,-i)\), verify \(Av=iv\) (or explain the correct \(\lambda\) if this \(v\) is for \(\lambda=-i\)).
Y4. True or false: every real \(2\times 2\) matrix has two real eigenvalues.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \((3-2i)(1+i)=3+3i-2i-2i^2=5+i\). Magnitude: \(|3-2i|=\sqrt{9+4}=\sqrt{13}\).
Y2. \(A-\lambda I=\begin{bmatrix}1-\lambda&2\\0&3-\lambda\end{bmatrix}\), so \(\det=(1-\lambda)(3-\lambda)\). Eigenvalues \(\lambda=1\) and \(\lambda=3\). For \(\lambda=3\): \((A-3I)v=\begin{bmatrix}-2&2\\0&0\end{bmatrix}v=0\) gives \(v_1=v_2\), e.g. \(v=(1,1)\).
Y3. \(Av=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-i\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}i\\1\end{bmatrix}\) and \(iv=\begin{bmatrix}i\\1\end{bmatrix}\). Yes — \(Av=iv\) (so this \(v\) matches \(\lambda=i\)).
Y4. False. The characteristic polynomial may have complex roots (e.g. \(90^\circ\) rotation: \(\lambda=\pm i\)).

title: Lecture 29 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Download PDF
Last updated: October 19, 2026.
Textbook: Boyd & Vandenberghe, VMLS (PDF)
Reading: Determinants (class notes). Related objectives: Lectures. Schedule.
Bring paper. Warm-up, fill-in notes, board examples, and Your turn.

title: Lecture 29 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compute determinants of \(2\times 2\) and simple triangular matrices.
Interpret determinant magnitude as area or volume scaling.
Connect determinant zero with lost dimension and noninvertibility.
Recognize the determinant of a triangular matrix from its diagonal.
Connect determinants to the coming characteristic equation.

title: Lecture 29 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}.
\]

What does \(x\mapsto Ax\) do to the unit square? What is the area of the image?
Are the columns of \(B\) independent? Guess whether \(B\) is invertible.

title: Lecture 29 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Fill in
For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}\), \[
\det A = ad-bc.
\] Geometrically, \(|\det A|\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) scaling factor of the unit square under \(x\mapsto Ax\) (signed area encodes orientation).
Triangular / diagonal. If \(T\) is upper or lower triangular (including diagonal), \[
\det T = \underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}.
\]
Invertibility. For square \(A\): \[
A\text{ invertible}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \det A \neq \underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}.
\] If \(\det A=0\), the image of the unit cube/square is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) (lost dimension): columns are dependent, \(Ax=b\) fails for some \(b\), and \(N(A)\) is nontrivial.
Product rule (preview). \(\det(AB)=(\det A)(\det B)\). Useful later for compositions.
Coming attraction. Eigenvalues solve \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) — the characteristic equation. Today’s \(\det\) is the tool; Week 13 builds the theory.

title: Lecture 29 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Worked in class
W1. Compute.

\(\det\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\det\begin{bmatrix}1&4&0\\0&-2&5\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\det\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&2\end{bmatrix}\)

W2. Area scaling. Let \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-2\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\). Compute \(\det A\). Where do \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) go? What area does the unit square map to?
W3. Zero determinant. Explain, in one sentence each, why \(\det\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}=0\) means (i) noninvertible and (ii) the image of the unit square has area zero.
W4. Link to Monday. For invertible \(2\times 2\) \(A\), the formula for \(A^{-1}\) has \(\det A\) in the denominator. What goes wrong if \(\det A=0\)?
W5. Characteristic preview. For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{bmatrix}\), expand \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) as a quadratic in \(\lambda\). (No need to “solve eigenvalues” yet — just form the polynomial.)

title: Lecture 29 — Determinants, geometry, and invertibility
text:
Your turn
Y1. Compute \(\det\begin{bmatrix}4&-1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}\) and \(\det\begin{bmatrix}-1&0&0\\2&5&0\\3&1&2\end{bmatrix}\).
Y2. Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,-1)\). What is \(|\det A|\)? Interpret as area scaling of the unit square.
Y3. True or false: if \(\det A=0\) for square \(A\), then \(Ax=b\) has either no solution or infinitely many solutions for every \(b\).






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(\det\begin{bmatrix}4&-1\\2&3\end{bmatrix}=12-(-2)=14\). Lower triangular: \(\det=(-1)(5)(2)=-10\).
Y2. \(|\det A|=|(2)(-1)|=2\): the unit square is mapped to a rectangle of area \(2\) (stretched by \(2\) horizontally and reflected/flipped vertically).
Y3. True. Singular means no unique solution for any \(b\): if \(b\in C(A)\) there are infinitely many solutions; otherwise none.

title: Lecture 27 — Inverses and solving
text:
Download PDF
Last updated: October 19, 2026.
Boyd video (optional): Lecture 30 — left & right inverses · ENGR108 playlist (Boyd)
Textbook: Boyd & Vandenberghe, VMLS (PDF)
Reading: Boyd 11.1–11.3. Related objectives: Lectures. Schedule.
Bring paper. Warm-up while attendance is taken, then fill-in notes, board examples, and Your turn.

title: Lecture 27 — Inverses and solving
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Interpret an inverse as undoing a transformation.
Determine whether a simple matrix is invertible.
Connect invertibility to uniqueness of \(Ax=b\).
Explain why solving \(Ax=b\) is generally preferable computationally to explicitly calculating \(A^{-1}\).

title: Lecture 27 — Inverses and solving
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Compute \(Ax\).
Can you find a matrix \(B\) such that \(B(Ax)=x\)? (Guess and check is fine for \(2\times 2\).) What would such a \(B\) “undo”?

title: Lecture 27 — Inverses and solving
text:
Fill in
A square matrix \(A\) is invertible (nonsingular) if there exists a matrix \(A^{-1}\) of the same size with \[
A^{-1}A = AA^{-1} = \underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}.
\] Then \(A^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(A\). Think of \(x\mapsto Ax\) as a map: \(A^{-1}\) is the map that \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) it.
Solving. If \(A\) is invertible, the unique solution of \(Ax=b\) is \[
x = \underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}.
\] Equivalently: \(Ax=b\) has a unique solution for every \(b\) if and only if \(A\) is invertible.
Quick \(2\times 2\) test. For \(A=\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}\), \[
A^{-1}=\frac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}
\] provided \(ad-bc\neq 0\). (We will call \(ad-bc\) the determinant on Friday.)
Compute carefully. Forming \(A^{-1}\) explicitly and then multiplying \(A^{-1}b\) is usually \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) than solving \(Ax=b\) by elimination / a solver. Prefer A\b / solve(A,b), not “invert then multiply,” unless you truly need many right-hand sides and already have a factorization.

title: Lecture 27 — Inverses and solving
text:
Worked in class
W1. Undo a map. Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1/2)\). What does \(x\mapsto Ax\) do geometrically? Write \(A^{-1}\) and check \(A^{-1}A=I\).
W2. Invertible or not? For each matrix, decide and give a one-line reason (try to solve \(Ax=0\), or use the \(2\times 2\) formula).

\(\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\)

W3. Unique solution. Suppose \(A\) is invertible and \(Ax=b\) and \(Ay=b\). Why must \(x=y\)?
W4. Solve, don’t invert. For \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}3\\4\end{bmatrix},
\] solve \(Ax=b\) by back substitution (no inverse needed). Then, if time, form \(A^{-1}\) and check \(A^{-1}b\) matches.
W5. Cost intuition. You need \(x\) for one \(b\). Which is the better default plan: (i) compute \(A^{-1}\) then \(A^{-1}b\), or (ii) solve \(Ax=b\) with a solver? One sentence.

title: Lecture 27 — Inverses and solving
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (\(90^\circ\) CCW). What matrix undoes \(R\)? Check by multiplying.
Y2. Is \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}\) invertible? Explain using \(Ax=b\) for a well-chosen \(b\), or using \(Ax=0\).
Y3. Suppose \(A\) is invertible and \(Ax=b\). True or false: if you change \(b\) to a different vector \(b'\), there is still exactly one solution \(x'\).
Y4. True or false, with a one-line reason: for a square system, computing \(x=A^{-1}b\) by first forming \(A^{-1}\) by hand is the recommended computational method in this course.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Rotation by \(90^\circ\) clockwise undoes CCW \(90^\circ\), so \[
R^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}
\] (equivalently \(R^{\mathsf{T}}\), or \(R^3\)). Check: \(R^{-1}R=I\).
Y2. Not invertible. Columns are dependent (second column is zero), so \(Ax=0\) has nontrivial solutions, e.g. \(x=(0,1)\). Equivalently, \(Ax=b\) fails for \(b=(0,1)\).
Y3. True. Invertibility means \(Ax=b'\) has the unique solution \(x'=A^{-1}b'\) for every right-hand side.
Y4. False. Prefer solving \(Ax=b\) (elimination / a solver). Explicit \(A^{-1}\) is usually more work and less stable for a single \(b\).

title: Lecture 25 — Composition and matrix powers
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Combine multistage processes using a matrix product.
Connect \(A^k x\) to repeated dynamics.
Interpret selected entries of a matrix product or power.
Recognize how network and transition information accumulates through powers.

title: Lecture 25 — Composition and matrix powers
Lecture 25 — Composition and matrix powers
text:
Fill in
Composition. If \(g(x)=Bx\) and \(f(y)=Ay\) (compatible sizes), then \[
(f\circ g)(x) = f(g(x)) = \underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}.
\] The matrix of the composed map is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) \(AB\) (apply \(B\) first). Multistage processes: write each stage as a matrix, then multiply in the right order.
Matrix powers. If \(A\) is square \(n\times n\), define \(A^0=I\), \(A^1=A\), and \[
A^{k} = \underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}
\] (\(k\) factors). Then \(A^{k+\ell}=A^k A^\ell\).
Dynamics connection. For \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) (Lab 4 / Lectures 24–26), \[
x_k = \underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}.
\] So iterating the recurrence \(k\) times is the same as one matrix–vector product with \(A^k\). Powers package “\(k\) steps of the system” into a single matrix.
Networks / paths. If \(A\) is an adjacency matrix (Boyd: \(A_{ij}=1\) means an edge from \(j\) to \(i\)), then \((A^k)_{ij}\) counts \(\underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}\) of length \(k\) from \(j\) to \(i\). Transition / population models: powers accumulate multi-step flow.

title: Lecture 25 — Composition and matrix powers
text:
Worked in class
W1. Multistage product. A population moves in two stages each year: migration \(B=\begin{bmatrix}0.8&0.1\\0.2&0.9\end{bmatrix}\), then growth/decay \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1.05,0.95)\). Write the one-year matrix \(M\) and compute \(M\begin{bmatrix}100\\100\end{bmatrix}\).
W2. Dynamics as a power. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.5&0.5\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad x_0=\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(x_1=Ax_0\), \(x_2=Ax_1\), and \(A^2\). Check that \(x_2=A^2 x_0\).
W3. Entry interpretation. Directed graph on nodes \(\{1,2,3\}\) with edges \(1\to 2\), \(2\to 3\), \(3\to 1\), and also \(1\to 3\). Adjacency (Boyd convention): \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 0 \\
1 & 1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(A^2\). What does \((A^2)_{31}\) mean? How many length-\(2\) walks from \(1\) to \(3\)?
W4. Why powers matter for Lab 4. In one sentence: if you already computed \(A^{10}\), how do you get \(x_{10}\) from \(x_0\) without looping ten times by hand?

title: Lecture 25 — Composition and matrix powers
text:
Your turn
Y1. Stage 1: \(B=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\). Stage 2: \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\). Find \(M\) for “\(B\) then \(A\)” and compute \(M(1,1)\).
Y2. With \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (swap coordinates) and \(x_0=(3,1)\), compute \(A^2\) and \(x_2=A^2 x_0\). Interpret \(A^2\).
Y3. Using the adjacency matrix \(A\) from W3, compute \((A^2)_{22}\). Interpret: walks of length \(2\) that start and end at node \(2\).
Y4. True or false: for the dynamics \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\), we always have \(x_{5}=A x_{4}\) and also \(x_{5}=A^{5}x_{0}\).






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(M=AB=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\2&0\end{bmatrix}\). Then \(M(1,1)=(-1,2)\).
Y2. \(A^2=I\) (swap twice returns to the start). \(x_2=A^2 x_0=(3,1)=x_0\). So \(A^2\) is the identity map — two swaps undo each other.
Y3. From W3, \[
A^2=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix},
\] so \((A^2)_{22}=0\): there is no walk of length \(2\) from \(2\) back to \(2\). (From \(2\) the only edge is \(2\to 3\); from \(3\) you go to \(1\), not back to \(2\) in one more step.)
Y4. True. Both follow from \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) by induction: one step from \(x_4\), and five steps packaged as \(A^5\).

title: Lecture 23 — From row operations to matrix products
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Apply an elementary matrix to an augmented matrix and read the solution set (including a parametric form).
Classify unique / none / infinitely many from RREF and write infinite families with a parameter \(t\).
Build a transition matrix from a two-compartment flow using a clear from/to convention, and compute one step \(x_1=Ax_0\).
Explain why two steps require \(A(Ax_0)\) — a matrix–matrix idea — and compute a small product \(AB\) by hand.
Give an example with \(AB\neq BA\), and compute \(A^2\) and a small power \(A^n x\).

title: Lecture 23 — From row operations to matrix products
text:
Warm-up
You already multiply matrices when you left-multiply an augmented matrix by an elementary matrix. Let \[
[A\mid b]=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&|&3\\ 2&4&|&6\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
E=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ -2&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] (\(E\) is “add \(-2\) times row 1 to row 2,” built by doing that operation to \(I\).)

Compute \(E\,[A\mid b]\).
Read off the solution set of the resulting system. (It should be infinitely many solutions.)

title: Lecture 23 — From row operations to matrix products
text:
Fill in

Solution types from RREF
After reducing \([A\mid b]\) to RREF, one of three things happens:








What you see in RREF
Conclusion
How to present the answer




A row \([0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c]\) with \(c\neq 0\)
\(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) solution
Write “inconsistent” / empty set


Pivot in every variable column; consistent
\(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) solution
Write the unique \(x\)


Consistent, and at least one free variable
\(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) solutions
Set each free variable equal to a parameter (\(t\), \(s\), …) and express the pivot variables in terms of those parameters



Parametric form (one free variable). If \(x_2\) is free, set \(x_2=t\) and solve for the others. The solution set is all vectors of the form \[
x=\underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}
\] as \(t\) runs over \(\mathbb{R}\).


Transition matrices (from / to)
A discrete linear dynamical system is \[
x_{t+1}=Ax_t.
\]
Convention used in this class (two compartments labeled \(1,2\)):

Columns = “from.” Column \(j\) is the next state if the current state is \(e_j\) (everyone starts in compartment \(j\)).
Rows = “to.” Entry \(A_{ij}\) is the fraction (or amount) that goes from \(j\) to \(i\).

So: read \(A_{ij}\) as “to \(i\), from \(j\).”
One step is matrix–vector multiplication: \(x_1=\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\). Two steps: \(x_2=A x_1=A(Ax_0)\). That is the same as \((AA)x_0\), so we need the matrix–matrix product \(A^2=AA\).


Matrix–matrix product
If \(A\) is \(m\times n\) and \(B\) is \(n\times p\), then \(AB\) is the \(m\times p\) matrix whose \(j\)th column is \[
(AB)_j=\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}.
\] Equivalently, entry \((i,j)\) is the inner product of row \(i\) of \(A\) with column \(j\) of \(B\).
Defined when? Number of \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\) of \(A\) equals number of \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\) of \(B\).
Not commutative. In general \(AB\neq BA\) (even when both are defined).
Powers. For a square matrix, \(A^2=AA\), \(A^3=A^2A=\cdots\), and \(x_n=A^n x_0\).

title: Lecture 23 — From row operations to matrix products
text:
Worked in class
W1. Unique solution. From the RREF \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&|&2\\
0&1&|&-1
\end{bmatrix},
\] write the solution.
W2. No solution. From the RREF \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1&2&|&3\\
0&0&|&1
\end{bmatrix},
\] explain why there is no solution.
W3. Infinitely many — parametrize. From the RREF \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1&2&0&|&3\\
0&0&1&|&-1
\end{bmatrix},
\] name the free variable, set it equal to \(t\), and write \(x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\) in terms of \(t\).
W4. Transition matrix. Two towns, Arcata and Eureka:

Of those in Arcata, \(80\%\) stay and \(20\%\) move to Eureka.
Of those in Eureka, \(90\%\) stay and \(10\%\) move to Arcata.

Order the state as \(x_t=(\text{Arcata},\text{Eureka})\). Using rows = to, columns = from, write \(A\). With \(x_0=(5000,7000)\), compute \(x_1=Ax_0\).
W5. One step vs two steps. Using the same \(A\) and \(x_0\) as W4:

Compute \(x_2=A x_1\) (another matrix–vector product).
Compute \(A^2=AA\) as a matrix–matrix product, then compute \(A^2 x_0\). Check that it matches \(x_2\).

W6. Product by hand. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\3&2\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(AB\) (columns \(Ab_1\), \(Ab_2\), or row–column dots).
W7. Order matters. With the same \(A\) and \(B\), compute \(BA\). Is \(BA=AB\)?
W8. Powers. Let \(C=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\).

Compute \(C^2\) and \(C^3\).
Guess \(C^n\), then check for \(n=2\) and \(n=3\). For \(x_0=(0,1)\), compute \(C^n x_0\).

title: Lecture 23 — From row operations to matrix products
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
[A\mid b]=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&|&2\\ 3&-3&|&6\end{bmatrix},\qquad
E=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ -3&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute \(E\,[A\mid b]\) and write the solution set with parameter \(t\).
Y2. From the RREF \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&-2&|&5\\
0&1&3&|&-1\\
0&0&0&|&0
\end{bmatrix},
\] write the general solution with free variable \(t=x_3\).
Y3. Build \(A\) for two labs, North and South:

From North: \(70\%\) stay, \(30\%\) go South.
From South: \(60\%\) stay, \(40\%\) go North.

State order \(x_t=(\text{North},\text{South})\). Write \(A\) (rows = to, columns = from). If \(x_0=(100,50)\), find \(x_1\).
Y4. Let \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\1&3\end{bmatrix}\) and \(x_0=(1,0)\). Compute \(x_1=Ax_0\) and \(x_2=A x_1\). Then compute \(A^2\) and \(A^2 x_0\).
Y5. With \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{bmatrix},
\] compute \(AB\) and \(BA\). Are they equal?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(E\,[A\mid b]=\begin{bmatrix}1&-1&|&2\\ 0&0&|&0\end{bmatrix}\). Free variable \(x_2=t\); then \(x_1-t=2\), so \(x_1=2+t\). Solution: \(x=(2+t,\,t)\) for \(t\in\mathbb{R}\).
Y2. Free \(x_3=t\). Then \(x_1-2t=5\) and \(x_2+3t=-1\), so \[
x=\begin{bmatrix}5+2t\\ -1-3t\\ t\end{bmatrix},\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Y3. Rows = to, columns = from (order North, South): \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.4\\ 0.3&0.6\end{bmatrix}.
\] (Column 1: from North; column 2: from South.) Then \[
x_1=Ax_0=\begin{bmatrix}0.7\cdot 100+0.4\cdot 50\\ 0.3\cdot 100+0.6\cdot 50\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}90\\ 60\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y4. \(x_1=(2,1)\), \(x_2=A x_1=(4,5)\). Also \[
A^2=\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\5&9\end{bmatrix},\qquad A^2 x_0=(4,5),
\] same as \(x_2\).
Y5. \[
AB=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
BA=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.
\] Not equal: \(AB\neq BA\).

title: Lecture 21 — Systems, \(Ax=b\), and elimination
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Translate equations into \(Ax=b\) and classify the system as square, overdetermined, or underdetermined.
Interpret \(Ax=b\) as asking whether \(b\) is in the span of the columns, and anticipate no solution, one solution, or infinitely many.
Match each elementary row operation with its matrix, use those matrices to eliminate, and solve a small system by back substitution.
Explain why those row operations preserve the solution set.

title: Lecture 21 — Systems, \(Ax=b\), and elimination
text:
Warm-up
For \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 - 2x_2 &= 3 \\
2x_1 + x_2 &= 1,
\end{aligned}
\] write \(A\), \(x\), \(b\), and the augmented matrix \([A\mid b]\). Is \(b\) in the span of the columns of \(A\)?

title: Lecture 21 — Systems, \(Ax=b\), and elimination
text:
Fill in
A linear system with \(m\) equations in \(n\) unknowns can be written \(Ax=b\), where \(A\) is \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\), \(x\) is an \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)-vector, and \(b\) is an \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)-vector.
Column view. Solving \(Ax=b\) asks: is \(b\) a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) of the columns of \(A\)? Equivalently: does \(b\) lie in \(\operatorname{span}\{\text{columns of }A\}\)?
Shape vocabulary (compare \(m\) equations to \(n\) unknowns):








Name
Relation
Typical intuition




Square
\(m=\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\)
Often one solution, but not always


Overdetermined
\(m>\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\)
Often \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (too many constraints)


Underdetermined
\(m<\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\)
Often \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (free variables)



These are tendencies, not guarantees. A square system can be inconsistent or have infinitely many solutions. An overdetermined system can still be consistent.
Possible outcomes for \(Ax=b\):

No solution — \(b\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) the column space.
Unique solution — \(b\) is in the column space in exactly \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\) way.
Infinitely many solutions — \(b\) is in the column space in \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) ways (free parameters).

The augmented matrix of \(Ax=b\) is \([A\mid b]\), with \(b\) as an extra \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\).
Elementary row operations that do not change the solution set:

\(\underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}\) two rows.
Multiply a row by a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) scalar. (Multiplying by \(0\) is not allowed: it is not reversible and can destroy an equation.)
Add a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of one row to another row.

Matrices for those operations. Left-multiplying \([A\mid b]\) by a matrix does the row operation. Build that matrix by doing the same operation to \(I\). For two equations:
Swap the two rows: \[
\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Multiply row 1 by \(c\neq 0\), or multiply row 2 by \(c\neq 0\): \[
\begin{bmatrix}c&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&c\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Add \(c\) times row 1 to row 2, or add \(c\) times row 2 to row 1: \[
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\c&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}1&c\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
The extra number sits in the row you are changing, in the column of the row you copy from. For three equations, start from \(I_3\) and edit that same spot. Adding \(2\) times row 1 to row 3 uses \[
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\2&0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Why they preserve solutions: each allowed operation is reversible, so the new system is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) to the old one. Each matrix above is invertible, which is the same fact in matrix language.
Gaussian elimination aims for echelon form: zeros \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) each pivot, pivots marching right as you go down. Then back substitution solves from the \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) equation upward. Reduced form, free variables, and software are next time.

title: Lecture 21 — Systems, \(Ax=b\), and elimination
text:
Worked in class
W1. Matrix form. Three unknowns \(x_1,x_2,x_3\): \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 + x_2 &= 4 \\
x_2 - x_3 &= 1 \\
2x_1 + x_3 &= 3.
\end{aligned}
\] Write \(A\), \(x\), and \(b\). Square / over / under?
W2. Span interpretation. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}3\\6\end{bmatrix},\quad
c=\begin{bmatrix}3\\5\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) Are the columns of \(A\) independent? Describe \(\operatorname{span}\{\text{columns}\}\). (b) Does \(Ax=b\) have a solution? Infinitely many? (c) Does \(Ax=c\) have a solution?
W3. Eliminate and back-substitute. Starting from \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & | & 5 \\
2 & 3 & | & 8
\end{bmatrix},
\] replace Row 2 by (Row 2) \(-\) \(2\cdot\)(Row 1). Solve for \(x_2\), then \(x_1\).
W4. Three operations, then a full solve by applying matrices. Start from the warm-up matrix \[
M=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&|&3\\2&1&|&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Swap the two rows: \[
\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}M
=\begin{bmatrix}2&1&|&1\\1&-2&|&3\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Multiply row 1 by \(2\): \[
\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}M
=\begin{bmatrix}2&-4&|&6\\2&1&|&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Add \(-2\) times row 1 to row 2. This is the elimination step: \[
E_1=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\-2&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
E_1 M=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&|&3\\0&5&|&-5\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Continue from \(E_1 M\) until the left side is \(I\). Multiply the new row 2 by \(\frac{1}{5}\): \[
E_2=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&\frac{1}{5}\end{bmatrix},\qquad
E_2 E_1 M=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&|&3\\0&1&|&-1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Add \(2\) times the new row 2 to row 1: \[
E_3=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
E_3 E_2 E_1 M=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&|&1\\0&1&|&-1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Read the solution \(x=(1,-1)\). The same three matrices clear \(A\) itself: \(E_3 E_2 E_1 A=I\). We name that product \(A^{-1}\) later.
W5 (if time). Anticipating outcomes. Without fully solving, say what you expect (and why):

\(2\) equations, \(2\) unknowns, with clearly parallel incompatible lines.
\(1\) equation, \(3\) unknowns: \(x_1+x_2+x_3=5\).
\(3\) equations, \(2\) unknowns that happen to be consistent (the third is the sum of the first two).

W6 (if time). Context \(\to Ax=b\). A café sells tea (\(\$2\)) and coffee (\(\$3\)). On Monday they sold \(x_1\) teas and \(x_2\) coffees for \(\$26\) total revenue, and sold \(10\) drinks in all. Write the two equations and the matrix form. Square?
W7 (if time). A \(3\times 3\) echelon. Reduce \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 1 & | & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 2 & | & 5 \\
2 & 1 & 0 & | & 5
\end{bmatrix}
\] to echelon form and decide whether a solution exists.

title: Lecture 21 — Systems, \(Ax=b\), and elimination
text:
Your turn
Start with Y1–Y4. Y5–Y9 are the elimination cousins if you finish.
Y1. Write as \(Ax=b\): \[
\begin{aligned}
3x_1 - x_2 &= 0 \\
x_1 + 4x_2 &= 7.
\end{aligned}
\] Classify as square / over / under.
Y2. Let \(A\) have columns \(a_1=(1,0,1)\) and \(a_2=(0,1,1)\). For \(b=(1,1,2)\), explain in one sentence why \(Ax=b\) has a solution, and give one solution \(x\).
Y3. True or false, with a one-line reason: every square system \(Ax=b\) has exactly one solution.
Y4. A sensor gives \(4\) linear measurements for \(2\) unknown parameters. Is the system typically overdetermined? Does that guarantee inconsistency?
Y5. Augmented matrix for \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 - x_2 &= 1 \\
3x_1 + 2x_2 &= 12.
\end{aligned}
\]
Y6. Clear the \((2,1)\) entry of \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
3 & 2 & | & 12
\end{bmatrix}
\] by a row replacement. Write the new matrix.
Y7. From the echelon form \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
0 & 5 & | & 9
\end{bmatrix},
\] solve by back substitution.
Y8. True or false, with a one-line reason: if you swap two rows of \([A\mid b]\), the solution set of \(Ax=b\) can change.
Y9. Write the \(2\times 2\) elementary matrix for each operation.

Multiply row 1 by \(4\).
Add \(3\) times row 2 to row 1.
Apply the matrix from (b) to \(\begin{bmatrix}1&0&|&2\\0&1&|&5\end{bmatrix}\).







NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\1&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}0\\7\end{bmatrix}.
\] Square (\(m=n=2\)).
Y2. \(b=1\cdot a_1+1\cdot a_2\), so \(b\) is in the column span; one solution is \(x=(1,1)\).
Y3. False. Square systems can be inconsistent (parallel lines) or have infinitely many solutions (the same line twice).
Y4. Typically overdetermined (\(m=4>n=2\)). No — consistency depends on whether \(b\) lands in the column space.
Y5. \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
3 & 2 & | & 12
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y6. Row2 \(\leftarrow\) Row2 \(-\) \(3\cdot\)Row1 gives \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & | & 1 \\
0 & 5 & | & 9
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y7. From Row 2: \(5x_2=9\) so \(x_2=9/5\). From Row 1: \(x_1-x_2=1\) so \(x_1=1+9/5=14/5\). Solution \(x=(14/5,\,9/5)\).
Y8. False. Swapping rows reorders equations and keeps the same solution set.
Y9. (a) \(\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). (b) \(\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). (c) Row 1 becomes \((1,0,2)+3(0,1,5)=(1,3,17)\), so \[
\begin{bmatrix}1&3&|&17\\0&1&|&5\end{bmatrix}.
\]

title: Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compute \(Ax\) by hand for a small matrix.
Interpret \(Ax\) as a linear combination of the columns of \(A\).
Interpret \(A\) as an input-output transformation.
Explain how the dimensions of \(A\) determine the input and output spaces.

title: Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,2)\) and \(b=(-1,1)\). Compute \(2a-3b\). (This is the same skill as “columns of \(A\) times entries of \(x\).”)

title: Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication
text:
Fill in
If \(A\) is \(m\times n\) and \(x\) is an \(n\)-vector, the product \(y=Ax\) is an \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\)-vector.
Row view. The \(i\)th entry of \(Ax\) is the inner product of \(x\) with the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(A\): \[
y_i = (\text{row }i)^{\mathsf{T}}x.
\]
Column view (main story). If \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) are the columns of \(A\), then \[
Ax = x_1 a_1 + x_2 a_2 + \cdots + x_n a_n.
\] So \(Ax\) is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) of the columns of \(A\), with coefficients from \(x\).
Dimensions: \(A\) maps inputs in \(\mathbb{R}^{\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}}\) to outputs in \(\mathbb{R}^{\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}}\). Thinking of \(A\) as a machine: feed in \(x\), get out \(Ax\).
Special cases: \(Ix=x\); \(0x=0\); if \(A=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)\), then \(Ax=(\lambda_1 x_1,\ldots,\lambda_n x_n)\).

title: Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication
text:
Worked in class
W1. Compute by hand. \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\ -1&3&1\end{bmatrix},\quad
x=\begin{bmatrix}2\\ 1\\ -1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Find \(Ax\) using both the row-inner-product view and the column-combination view.
W2. Same \(A\), different \(x\). Without recomputing from scratch: if you already know \(Ax\) from W1, what is \(A(2x)\)? What is \(A(x+e_1)\) if \(e_1=(1,0,0)\)? (Use linearity / columns.)
W3. Input-output story. A \(2\times 2\) matrix \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.9&0.2\\ 0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix}
\] sends (urban, rural) population fractions today to tomorrow. If \(x=(0.6,0.4)\), compute \(Ax\) and interpret the two output entries.
W4. Dimension mismatch. Can you form \(Ax\) if \(A\) is \(3\times 2\) and \(x\) is a \(3\)-vector? What size must \(x\) be?

title: Lecture 19 — Matrix-vector multiplication
text:
Your turn
Y1. Compute \[
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & -1 \\
0 & 3 \\
1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
4 \\ -2
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y2. Let \(A\) have columns \(a_1=(1,0,1)\) and \(a_2=(0,1,1)\). Write \(A\) explicitly. For \(x=(3,-2)\), express \(Ax\) as a linear combination of \(a_1,a_2\), then evaluate.
Y3. True or false: if \(A\) is \(m\times n\), then \(Ax\) is always in the span of the columns of \(A\).
Y4. A sensor turns a \(3\)-vector of raw readings \(x\) into a \(2\)-vector of summaries via \(Ax\). What are the dimensions of \(A\)? In one sentence, what do the columns of \(A\) mean?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \((2)(4)+(-1)(-2)=10\); \((0)(4)+(3)(-2)=-6\); \((1)(4)+(1)(-2)=2\). So \(Ax=(10,-6,2)\).
Y2. \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\\1&1\end{bmatrix}\). \(Ax=3a_1-2a_2=(3,-2,1)\).
Y3. True. By the column interpretation, \(Ax\) is always a linear combination of the columns.
Y4. \(A\) is \(2\times 3\). The \(j\)th column is the summary \(2\)-vector produced when the input is the standard unit vector \(e_j\) (effect of “only feature \(j\) active”).

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Define span using linear combinations.
Determine whether a vector lies in a simple span.
Interpret spans geometrically as lines, planes, or higher-dimensional collections.
Recognize basic subspaces and distinguish them from shifted lines or planes.

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,0)\) and \(b=(0,1)\). Can you write \(v=(3,-2)\) as \(\alpha a+\beta b\)? If yes, give \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\).

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Fill in
The span of vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\) is the set of all linear combinations \[
\operatorname{span}\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}
  = \{\, \beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k \mid \beta_i\in\mathbb{R} \,\}.
\] So \(v\) lies in the span iff the equation \(\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k=v\) has \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
Geometry (in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) or \(\mathbb{R}^3\)):

Span of one nonzero vector: a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) through the origin.
Span of two non-parallel vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^3\): a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) through the origin.
Span of the standard basis of \(\mathbb{R}^n\): all of \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\).

A subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a nonempty set \(V\) closed under addition and scalar multiplication (equivalently: closed under linear combinations). Every subspace contains \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
Spans are always subspaces. A line or plane that does not pass through the origin is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) a subspace (it fails to contain \(0\), or fails closure under scaling).
Independence vs span: an independent list that spans \(V\) will be called a basis of \(V\) next class. Today, focus on “can I build \(v\) from these vectors?”

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Worked in class
W1. Membership. Let \(a=(1,1)\) and \(b=(1,-1)\).

Is \(v=(2,0)\) in \(\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}\)? Find coefficients or explain why not.
Is \(w=(1,0,0)\) in \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,1,0),(0,1,1)\}\) inside \(\mathbb{R}^3\)?

W2. Geometry. Sketch in \(\mathbb{R}^2\): \(\operatorname{span}\{(2,1)\}\) and \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,0),(0,1)\}\).
W3. Subspace check. Which of the following are subspaces of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)? Brief reason.

All vectors \((x,y)\) with \(y=3x\).
All vectors \((x,y)\) with \(y=3x+1\).
The single point \(\{(0,0)\}\).
All vectors with \(\lVert(x,y)\rVert=1\) (the unit circle).

W4. Dependent generators. Let \(a=(1,0)\), \(b=(2,0)\), \(c=(0,1)\). Explain why \(\operatorname{span}\{a,b,c\}=\operatorname{span}\{a,c\}\). What does that say about redundant generators?
W5. Application. Two feature directions \(f_1=\)“morning temperature pattern” and \(f_2=\)“afternoon pattern” as \(24\)-vectors. What does it mean if a third pattern \(g\) lies in \(\operatorname{span}\{f_1,f_2\}\)?

title: Lecture 13 — Span, independence, and subspaces
text:
Check yourself
C1. Complete: \(v\in\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}\) means \(v=\underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}\) for some scalars.
C2. Is \((3,3)\) in \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,1)\}\)? Coefficients if yes.
C3. True or false: every subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a span of some list of vectors.
C4. Why is the set of vectors with first entry equal to \(1\) not a subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)?
C5. Give a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) that is not in \(\operatorname{span}\{(1,2)\}\).






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. \(v=\alpha a+\beta b\) (any equivalent wording).
C2. Yes. \((3,3)=3\cdot(1,1)\).
C3. True (in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) every subspace has a basis, hence is a span). For this course it is enough to know that the subspaces we meet are spans.
C4. It does not contain \(0\) (first entry would be \(0\)), or equivalently it is not closed under scaling.
C5. Example: \((1,0)\), or \((2,1)\), or any vector not a multiple of \((1,2)\).

title: Lecture 09 — Nearest neighbors
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Formulate a nearest-neighbor question using vectors.
Find a nearest neighbor in a small dataset by hand.
Explain how feature scale can affect the answer.
Justify a choice of distance or similarity measure.

title: Lecture 09 — Nearest neighbors
text:
Warm-up
Patients as 2-vectors (fever °F above 98.6, cough score 0–10): \[
p=(1.2,\ 3),\quad q=(0.1,\ 8),\quad r=(1.0,\ 4).
\] A new patient is \(x=(1.1,\ 3.5)\). Which of \(p,q,r\) is nearest to \(x\) in Euclidean distance? Compute the three distances.

title: Lecture 09 — Nearest neighbors
text:
Fill in
Given candidates \(z_1,\ldots,z_m\) and a query \(x\), a (distance) nearest neighbor is any \(z_j\) with \[
\lVert x-z_j\rVert \leq \lVert x-z_i\rVert \quad\text{for all }i.
\] In words: the candidate with \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) Euclidean distance to \(x\).
An angle nearest neighbor minimizes \(\angle(x,z_i)\) instead (equivalently maximizes cosine similarity when angles are in \([0,\pi]\)).
Feature vectors often mix units (age, dollars, counts). Then \(\lVert x-y\rVert^2\) adds \(\underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}\) of entrywise differences, so a large-scale feature can \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) the distance. Remedies include choosing units carefully, \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) features, or using a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) (Boyd 3.28).
Choose Euclidean distance when “close in feature space” means similar \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\). Choose angle/cosine when overall \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) should not matter (documents, some sensors).

title: Lecture 09 — Nearest neighbors
text:
Software
Octave — distances from x to rows of a matrix Z (one candidate per row):
x = [1.1; 3.5];
Z = [1.2, 3; 0.1, 8; 1.0, 4];   % each row a candidate
d = sqrt(sum((Z - x').^2, 2))  % 3 distances
[~, j] = min(d)                % nearest index
Python:
import numpy as np
x = np.array([1.1, 3.5])
Z = np.array([[1.2, 3.0], [0.1, 8.0], [1.0, 4.0]])
d = np.linalg.norm(Z - x, axis=1)
j = np.argmin(d)

title: Lecture 09 — Nearest neighbors
text:
Worked in class
W1. Formulate. “Among yesterday’s five Arcata weather vectors, which day is most like today?” Write this as a nearest-neighbor problem: what are \(x\) and \(z_1,\ldots,z_5\), and what distance will you use?
W2. Five candidates (Quiz 3 C1.1). \(x=(2,1)\) and \[
z_1=(2,2),\ z_2=(0,1),\ z_3=(3,1),\ z_4=(2,0),\ z_5=(1.5,1.5).
\] Compute all five distances and name the nearest neighbor.
W3. Rescale one feature (Quiz 3 C1.2). Same points, but replace the first coordinate by \(10\) times its value (so \(x\) becomes \((20,1)\), etc.). Recompute nearest neighbor. Did it change?
W4. EHR story (Boyd 3.11). In one or two sentences, give a practical use for finding the 10 nearest neighbors of a patient’s feature vector among other patients.
W5. Nearest nonnegative vector (Boyd 3.13 idea). For \(x=(3,-2,0.5,-4)\), what nonnegative \(y\) minimizes \(\lVert x-y\rVert\)? (Entrywise: you cannot do better than clipping negatives to \(0\).)

title: Lecture 09 — Nearest neighbors
text:
Check yourself
C1. \(x=(0,0)\), candidates \((1,0)\), \((0,2)\), \((0.5,0.5)\). Nearest?
C2. Why might cosine similarity beat Euclidean distance for bag-of-words document vectors?
C3. After standardizing every feature (mean \(0\), std \(1\) across the dataset), what problem with heterogeneous units have you partly addressed?
C4. True or false: the nearest neighbor is always unique.
C5. Write Octave or Python that prints the index of the nearest row of Z to x.






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. Distances \(1\), \(2\), \(\sqrt{0.5}\approx 0.707\). Nearest is \((0.5,0.5)\).
C2. Document length (total words) varies a lot; cosine compares direction of the word pattern and ignores overall scale.
C3. Features no longer live on wildly different numeric scales, so one feature is less likely to dominate Euclidean distance.
C4. False. Two candidates can tie for smallest distance.
C5. Octave: [~,j]=min(sqrt(sum((Z-x').^2,2))). Python: j=np.argmin(np.linalg.norm(Z-x,axis=1)).

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compute vector norms and distances.
Interpret norm and distance geometrically and contextually.
Relate norm to RMS and, where appropriate, variation around an average.
Use software to calculate distances in dimensions too large for hand computation.

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Warm-up
Let \(u=(3,-4)\) and \(v=(0,5)\).

Compute \(u^{\mathsf{T}}u\) and \(\sqrt{u^{\mathsf{T}}u}\) by hand.
Without a calculator, which is larger: \(\lVert u\rVert\) or \(\lVert v\rVert\)? Brief reason.

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Fill in
The Euclidean norm of an \(n\)-vector \(x\) is \[
\lVert x\rVert = \sqrt{x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2} = \sqrt{\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}}.
\] It measures the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(x\). For a scalar, \(\lVert x\rVert\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
Key properties (same size vectors; \(\beta\) a scalar): - \(\lVert \beta x\rVert = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\,\lVert x\rVert\) - \(\lVert x+y\rVert \leq \lVert x\rVert + \lVert y\rVert\) (triangle inequality) - \(\lVert x\rVert \geq 0\), and \(\lVert x\rVert=0\) only when \(x=\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\)
The RMS (root-mean-square) value is \[
\mathrm{rms}(x) = \frac{\lVert x\rVert}{\sqrt{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{x_1^2+\cdots+x_n^2}{n}}.
\] It describes a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) size of an entry, and is useful when comparing vectors of different \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
The distance between \(n\)-vectors \(a\) and \(b\) is \[
\mathrm{dist}(a,b) = \lVert a-b\rVert.
\] Geometrically this is the length of the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) from \(a\) to \(b\). Two vectors are “close” when this distance is \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (relative to the application).
The average is \(\mathrm{avg}(x)=\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}x\). The de-meaned vector is \(\tilde{x}=x-\mathrm{avg}(x)\mathbf{1}\). The standard deviation is \[
\mathrm{std}(x)=\mathrm{rms}(\tilde{x})=\frac{\lVert x-\mathrm{avg}(x)\mathbf{1}\rVert}{\sqrt{n}},
\] which measures typical \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) of the entries from their average.
Boyd’s identity: \(\mathrm{rms}(x)^2 = \mathrm{avg}(x)^2 + \mathrm{std}(x)^2\).

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Software (keep this page open)
In this course we use either Octave or Python for norms and distances.
Octave (column vectors are fine):
x = [3; -4; 0];
norm(x)                 % Euclidean norm
sqrt(x'*x)              % same idea via the inner product
y = [1; 2; -1];
norm(x-y)               % distance ||x-y||
Python (NumPy):
import numpy as np
x = np.array([3.0, -4.0, 0.0])
np.linalg.norm(x)       # Euclidean norm
np.sqrt(x @ x)          # same idea via the inner product
y = np.array([1.0, 2.0, -1.0])
np.linalg.norm(x - y)   # distance ||x-y||
Handy formulas (either language): - \(\mathrm{rms}(x)=\lVert x\rVert/\sqrt{n}\) - \(\mathrm{avg}(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_i\) (Octave mean(x), Python np.mean(x)) - \(\mathrm{std}(x)\) in Boyd’s sense is the RMS of the de-meaned vector (population form with divisor \(n\), not \(n-1\))

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Worked in class
W1. Norm by hand and by software (Lachniet-style). Let \[
u = (2,\ -4,\ 0).
\] (a) Compute \(\lVert u\rVert\) by hand using \(\sqrt{u^{\mathsf{T}}u}\).

Write the Octave command and the Python command that compute the same value. What should both print?
Form the unit vector \(\hat{u}=u/\lVert u\rVert\). What is \(\lVert\hat{u}\rVert\)?

W2. Distance and nearest neighbor (Quiz 3 / Boyd 3.10–3.11 style). Arcata morning temperatures (°F) for three days: \[
a=(52,51,53),\qquad b=(54,50,55),\qquad c=(60,58,59).
\] A new day is \(x=(53,52,54)\).

Compute \(\lVert x-a\rVert\), \(\lVert x-b\rVert\), and \(\lVert x-c\rVert\) by hand or with software.
Which day is the nearest neighbor of \(x\)?
In one sentence, what does “nearest” mean here?

W3. Boolean distance (Boyd 3.1). Suppose \(x\) and \(y\) are Boolean \(n\)-vectors (entries only \(0\) or \(1\)).

Show that \(\lVert x-y\rVert^2\) equals the number of positions where \(x\) and \(y\) disagree.
Therefore \(\lVert x-y\rVert=\sqrt{k}\) where \(k\) is that disagreement count. For \(x=(1,0,1,1,0)\) and \(y=(1,1,0,1,0)\), find \(k\) and \(\lVert x-y\rVert\).

W4. RMS, average, and standard deviation (Boyd 3.15 setup). Let \[
x=(2,4,4,6).
\] (a) Compute \(\mathrm{avg}(x)\), \(\lVert x\rVert\), \(\mathrm{rms}(x)\), the de-meaned vector \(\tilde{x}\), and \(\mathrm{std}(x)\).

Check Boyd’s identity \(\mathrm{rms}(x)^2=\mathrm{avg}(x)^2+\mathrm{std}(x)^2\).
Interpret \(\mathrm{std}(x)\) in one short sentence for this data.

W5. Feature scale changes nearest neighbor (Quiz 3 C1.2 style). Two features: area (in \(1000\) ft²) and bedrooms. Houses: \[
h_1=(1.6,\ 2),\qquad h_2=(1.5,\ 2),\qquad h_3=(1.6,\ 4).
\] (a) Compute \(\lVert h_1-h_2\rVert\) and \(\lVert h_1-h_3\rVert\). Which house is nearer to \(h_1\)?

Now measure area in square feet instead, so the vectors become \[
\tilde{h}_1=(1600,\ 2),\qquad \tilde{h}_2=(1500,\ 2),\qquad \tilde{h}_3=(1600,\ 4).
\] Compute \(\lVert\tilde{h}_1-\tilde{h}_2\rVert\) and \(\lVert\tilde{h}_1-\tilde{h}_3\rVert\). Which house is nearer to \(\tilde{h}_1\) now?
What changed, and why does Boyd warn about units on heterogeneous features?

title: Lecture 07 — Norm, distance, RMS, and variation
text:
Check yourself
C1. Let \(w=(1,-2,2)\). Compute \(\lVert w\rVert\) by hand. Then write one Octave line and one Python line that compute it.
C2. Quiz 3 C1.1 style. Observation \(x=(1,2)\). Candidates: \[
z_1=(0,2),\quad z_2=(3,2),\quad z_3=(1,5),\quad z_4=(2,1),\quad z_5=(1,2.5).
\] Compute the five distances \(\lVert x-z_i\rVert\) (hand or software). Which candidate is nearest?
C3. Boyd 3.2 style. Let \(a\) be an \(n\)-vector and \(b\) an \(m\)-vector, and set \(x=(a,b)\) (stack). Express \(\mathrm{rms}(x)\) in terms of \(\mathrm{rms}(a)\), \(\mathrm{rms}(b)\), \(n\), and \(m\).
C4. For \(t=(10,10,10,14)\), find \(\mathrm{avg}(t)\) and \(\mathrm{std}(t)\). Use Boyd’s definition (RMS of the de-meaned vector).
C5. True or false, with one sentence: if \(\lVert x\rVert=\lVert y\rVert\), then \(x=y\) or \(x=-y\).






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. \(\lVert w\rVert=\sqrt{1+4+4}=3\). Octave: norm([1;-2;2]). Python: np.linalg.norm(np.array([1.,-2.,2.])).
C2. Distances: \(1\), \(2\), \(3\), \(\sqrt{2}\approx 1.414\), \(0.5\). Nearest is \(z_5=(1,2.5)\).
C3. \(\mathrm{rms}(x)=\sqrt{\dfrac{n\,\mathrm{rms}(a)^2+m\,\mathrm{rms}(b)^2}{n+m}}\).
C4. \(\mathrm{avg}(t)=11\). De-meaned \((-1,-1,-1,3)\); \(\mathrm{std}(t)=\sqrt{(1+1+1+9)/4}=\sqrt{3}\).
C5. False. Example: \(x=(1,0)\) and \(y=(0,1)\) have the same norm but are neither equal nor negatives.

title: Lecture 05 — Linear and affine functions
text:
Download PDF

title: Lecture 05 — Linear and affine functions
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Distinguish linear from affine functions in examples.
Test superposition numerically on simple functions.
Construct a function \(a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) for a contextual quantity.
Evaluate a model by hand and computationally.

title: Lecture 05 — Linear and affine functions
text:
Fill in
A function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}\) is linear if for all \(n\)-vectors \(x,y\) and scalars \(\alpha,\beta\), \[
f(\alpha x + \beta y) = \alpha f(x) + \beta f(y).
\] This property is called \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
Equivalently, linear functions satisfy homogeneity \(f(\alpha x)=\alpha f(x)\) and additivity \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\).
Every linear function can be written as an inner product: \(f(x) = \underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) for some fixed \(n\)-vector \(a\).
A function is affine if it has the form \(f(x) = a^{\mathsf{T}}x + b\) for some \(n\)-vector \(a\) and scalar \(b\). The number \(b\) is the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) (or intercept).
Affine functions satisfy a restricted superposition rule: \(f(\alpha x + \beta y) = \alpha f(x) + \beta f(y)\) only when \(\alpha + \beta = \underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\).
If \(b \neq 0\), the function \(f(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) is affine but \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) linear.
The average \(\mathrm{avg}(x)=\frac{1}{n}(x_1+\cdots+x_n)\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\); the maximum entry \(\max(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\) is not (for \(n\geq 2\)).
A regression model \(\hat{y} = \beta^{\mathsf{T}}x + v\) predicts a scalar from features \(x\). The entry \(\beta_i\) tells how \(\hat{y}\) changes when feature \(x_i\) increases by one, holding other features fixed. The offset \(v\) is the predicted value when \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\).

title: Lecture 05 — Linear and affine functions
text:
Worked in class
W1. Classify each function below as linear, affine but not linear, or neither. If linear, write \(f(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x\).

\(f(x)=x_n-x_1\) (Boyd 2.1(b)).
\(f(x)=3x_1-2x_2+7\).
\(f(x)=\max(x_1,x_2)\) for \(n=2\).

W2. Superposition check. For \(f(x)=\max(x_1,x_2)\), let \(x=(1,-1)\), \(y=(-1,1)\), \(\alpha=\beta=\tfrac{1}{2}\). Compute \(f(\alpha x+\beta y)\) and \(\alpha f(x)+\beta f(y)\). What does this show?
W3. A 10-vector \(r\) stores course grades: \(r_1,\ldots,r_8\) are homework scores (0–10 each), \(r_9\) is midterm (0–120), \(r_10\) is final (0–160). Total score on 0–100 is 25% homework, 35% midterm, 40% final. Write \(s=w^{\mathsf{T}}r\) and give \(w\) (Boyd 1.10 style).
W4. Profit per unit is \(p=(4,2,-1)\) dollars for three items (item 3 is a loss leader). Monthly sales are \(s=(100,50,30)\) units. Total profit is \(p^{\mathsf{T}}s\) (Boyd 1.8). Compute it and interpret item 3’s sign.

title: Lecture 05 — Linear and affine functions
text:
Check yourself
C1. Boyd 2.1(a): \(f(x)=\max_k x_k - \min_k x_k\) (spread). Linear or not? One sentence why.
C2. Boyd 2.1(e): \(f(x)=x_n+(x_n-x_{n-1})\) (extrapolation). Linear or not? If linear, find \(a\) with \(f(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x\).
C3. Is \(g(x)=2x_1-x_3+5\) linear, affine, or neither? Write it as \(a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) if affine.
C4. Lachniet Ch. 1 Ex. 2(b): \(u=(2,-4,0)\), \(v=(3,1.5,-7)\). Find \(d=u^{\mathsf{T}}v\) (dot product). What does \(d=0\) suggest about direction?
C5. A café bill is \(f(x)=p^{\mathsf{T}}x\) with \(p=(3.50,2.00,1.25)\) and \(x=(2,1,0)\) (drinks ordered). Compute \(f(x)\) and state whether \(f\) is linear or affine.






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. Not linear (nor affine): spread fails superposition (Boyd uses \(x=(1,-1)\), \(y=(-1,1)\), \(\alpha=\beta=1/2\)).
C2. Linear: \(f(x)=x_n+(x_n-x_{n-1})=2x_n-x_{n-1}\), so \(a=(0,\ldots,0,-1,2)\) with \(a_{n-1}=-1\), \(a_n=2\).
C3. Affine but not linear: \(a=(2,0,-1)^{\mathsf{T}}\), \(b=5\).
C4. \(d=2\cdot 3+(-4)\cdot 1.5+0=6-6=0\). The vectors are orthogonal (perpendicular in 3D).
C5. \(f(x)=3.50\cdot 2+2.00\cdot 1+1.25\cdot 0=9.00\) dollars. Linear (also affine with \(b=0\)).

title: Lecture 03 — Linear combinations
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Form and interpret linear combinations.
Explain the meaning of coefficients in context.
Enter, index, and modify vectors in Octave or Python.
Perform vector arithmetic and create a basic plot.
Modify supplied code and explain its output or error message.

title: Lecture 03 — Linear combinations
text:
Warm-up
From Lecture 02, compute \[
2(3,-1)+(-1)(1,4).
\] Is the result a scalar or a vector? What is its length \(n\)?

title: Lecture 03 — Linear combinations
text:
Fill in
If \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) are \(n\)-vectors and \(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m\) are scalars, the vector \[
\beta_1 a_1 + \cdots + \beta_m a_m
\] is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) of \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\). The numbers \(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m\) are the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
Any \(n\)-vector \(b\) can be written using the standard unit vectors: \[
b = \underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}.
\]
The sum \(a_1+\cdots+a_m\) is the linear combination whose coefficients are all \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\). The average is the linear combination whose coefficients are all \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\).
A coefficient \(\beta_i\) means \(\underline{\hspace{4.0cm}}\) in context (for example: how many copies of a recipe, how far to walk in a direction, how loud to mix a track).

title: Lecture 03 — Linear combinations
text:
Worked in class
W1. Compute \(2(1,0)+(-1)(0,1)\) and sketch the result in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).
W2. Two shopping lists, in the order (apples, bread, milk): \[
x = (4, 1, 2), \qquad y = (1, 0, 1).
\] Interpret \(2x+y\) as “two copies of list \(x\), plus list \(y\).” Compute it. What would the coefficient \(-1\) in front of \(y\) mean?
W3. Write \((3,-1)\) as a linear combination of \(e_1\) and \(e_2\).

title: Lecture 03 — Linear combinations
text:
Your turn
Y1. Compute \(3(2,1,-1)+2(0,1,1)\).
Y2. Let \(u=(1,1)\) and \(v=(1,-1)\). Find coefficients \(\beta,\gamma\) so that \(\beta u+\gamma v=(4,2)\), or show your system of two equations. (We will finish the algebra together if time is short.)
Y3. Lab preview (Boyd indexes from 1). If \(x=(5,2,9)\), what is \(x_2\) in Boyd’s notation? In 1-based software (Octave), which command prints that entry? In 0-based software (Python/NumPy), which index prints that entry?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \((6,5,-1)\).
Y2. \(\beta u+\gamma v=(\beta+\gamma,\beta-\gamma)=(4,2)\), so \(\beta=3\), \(\gamma=1\). Check: \(3(1,1)+1(1,-1)=(4,2)\).
Y3. \(x_2=2\). Octave: x(2). Python: x[1].

title: Lecture 03 — Linear combinations
text:
Answers (Your turn)
Y1. \((6,5,-1)\).
Y2. \(\beta u+\gamma v=(\beta+\gamma,\beta-\gamma)=(4,2)\), so \(\beta=3\), \(\gamma=1\). Check: \(3(1,1)+1(1,-1)=(4,2)\).
Y3. \(x_2=2\). Octave: x(2). Python: x[1].
