title: Lecture 02 — Vector arithmetic and geometry
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Add, subtract, and scale vectors.
Interpret those operations geometrically.
Plot vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and recognize corresponding operations in \(\mathbb{R}^3\).
Check whether an answer has sensible dimensions and units.

title: Lecture 02 — Vector arithmetic and geometry
text:
Warm-up
Yesterday’s highs (Mon–Thu), in °F, were \[
t = (63, 59, 61, 66).
\] What is \(n\)? What is \(t_2\), and what does it mean? Is \(61\) a scalar or a vector? Write the 4-vector of “each day five degrees cooler than \(t\)” if you already know how — otherwise leave it blank and we will return to it.

title: Lecture 02 — Vector arithmetic and geometry
text:
Fill in
If \(a\) and \(b\) are \(n\)-vectors, the sum \(a+b\) is the \(n\)-vector whose \(i\)th entry is \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\). Addition is only defined when \(\underline{\hspace{3.0cm}}\).
The identity for addition is \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\): \(a+0=a\). The difference \(a-b\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
If \(\beta\) is a scalar, the scalar–vector product \(\beta a\) is the \(n\)-vector whose \(i\)th entry is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\). In particular, \((-1)a\) is written \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\).
Geometry in \(\mathbb{R}^2\): draw \(a\) as an arrow. Then \(\beta a\) with \(\beta>0\) points \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) and has length scaled by \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\). If \(\beta<0\), the arrow points \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\). The sum \(a+b\) can be drawn tip-to-tail or as the diagonal of a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
The same formulas work entrywise in \(\mathbb{R}^3\); we just cannot sketch as easily on paper.
Adding a scalar to a vector is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) in the mathematics of this course (even if some software will do it). Concatenating \((1,2)\) with \((3,4)\) is also \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) vector addition.

title: Lecture 02 — Vector arithmetic and geometry
text:
Worked in class
W1. A point on the quad is \(p=(2,1)\) (east, north, in 10 m units). A walk is the displacement \(a=(3,-1)\). Compute \(p+a\) and sketch \(p\), \(a\), and \(p+a\) in \(\mathbb{R}^2\). Then compute \(a-p\). Does \(a-p\) have the same units as \(p\)?
W2. Two rain gauges, in inches, over three days: \[
r = (0.40, 0, 1.10), \qquad s = (0.15, 0.20, 0.30).
\] Compute \(r+s\) and \(2r\). Why is \(r+(1,1)\) not a valid vector sum here? (These are 3-vectors: same arithmetic as in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), just one more entry.)
W3. Sanity check: can you form \((4,1)+(0,2,5)\)? Can you form \((18\text{ cm}, 4\text{ mm})+(1,1)\) as a meaningful measurement vector?

title: Lecture 02 — Vector arithmetic and geometry
text:
Your turn
Y1. Compute \[
\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(-2)
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0.5 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Y2. In \(\mathbb{R}^2\), sketch \(u=(3,1)\) and \(\tfrac{1}{2}u\). In words, what did scaling by \(1/2\) do? What would \(-u\) look like?
Y3. A 2-vector of temperatures in °C is \(x=(10, 14)\). A classmate types \(x+5\) in software and gets \((15,19)\). Is that the same as a vector sum \(x+v\) for some 2-vector \(v\)? If you need “five degrees warmer each day,” what vector should you add?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \((5,2,0)\) and \((-2,-1)\).
Y2. \(\tfrac{1}{2}u\) is the same direction, half as long. \(-u\) is the opposite direction, same length.
Y3. Software added the scalar \(5\) to each entry; that is not a vector–vector sum. Adding five degrees each day is the vector sum \(x+(5,5)\).

title: Lecture 04 — Inner product
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compute a dot product.
Interpret it as a weighted sum.
Interpret its sign and magnitude as alignment.
Recognize orthogonal vectors from a zero dot product.

title: Lecture 04 — Inner product
text:
Fill in — stack and slice
A stacked (or block) vector lists the entries of one vector after another. If \(b\) is an \(m\)-vector and \(c\) is an \(n\)-vector, then \[
(b, c) = (b_1,\ldots,b_m,\ c_1,\ldots,c_n)
\] is an \((m+n)\)-vector. A scalar can be stacked with a vector: if \(a\) is a 3-vector, then \((1,a)\) is a \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\)-vector with first entry \(1\), then \(a_1,a_2,a_3\).
Stacking is not vector addition: \((a,b)\) has length \(m+n\), not \(m\).
A slice (or subvector) takes a contiguous block of entries. Boyd’s notation \(x_{r:s}\) means the vector of entries \(x_r, x_{r+1}, \ldots, x_s\). It has length \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\). The endpoints are inclusive.
Example: if \(z=(1,-1,2,0)\), then \(z_{2:3} = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
If \(a\) and \(b\) are 10-vectors and \(c\) is a 20-vector, then \((a,b,c_{3:13})\) has length \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).

title: Lecture 04 — Inner product
text:
Fill in
For \(n\)-vectors \(a\) and \(b\), the inner product (or dot product) is the scalar \[
a^{\mathsf{T}}b = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + \cdots + a_n b_n = \sum_{i=1}^n \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}.
\] It is only defined when \(a\) and \(b\) have the same \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\).
If \(w\) is a weight vector and \(x\) is a data vector (same length), then \(w^{\mathsf{T}}x\) is a \(\underline{\hspace{3.2cm}}\) of the entries of \(x\), using the weights in \(w\).
Geometrically in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (and similarly in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)): if \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b>0\), the arrows point roughly the \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) direction; if \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b<0\), they point roughly \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) directions; if \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b=0\), the vectors are \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
Two vectors with \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b=0\) are orthogonal (perpendicular). The inner product is commutative: \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b = \underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
The quantity \(a^{\mathsf{T}}a = a_1^2 + \cdots + a_n^2\) is always \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) (never negative).

title: Lecture 04 — Inner product
text:
Worked in class
W1. Let \(b=(2,-1)\) and \(c=(0,3,1)\). Write the stacked vector \((b,c)\) explicitly. What is its length?
W2. Let \(z=(1,-1,2,0)\). Write \(z_{2:3}\) and \(z_{1:2}\). If \(x=(63,59,61,66)\) is four daily high temperatures (°F), write the 3-vector of day-to-day changes as \(x_{2:4} - x_{1:3}\).
W3. Compute \(u^{\mathsf{T}}v\) for \(u=(1,1)\) and \(v=(1,-1)\). Sketch both arrows in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) from the origin. How does the zero dot product match the picture?
W4. Three quiz parts have scores (out of 1): \[
g = (0.80,\ 0.90,\ 0.70),
\] with weights \[
w = (0.50,\ 0.30,\ 0.20).
\] Compute the weighted total \(w^{\mathsf{T}}g\). (Same idea as a weighted average when the weights sum to 1.)
W5. Morning wind displacements (east, north), in km/h: \[
a = (3, 1), \qquad b = (-1, 3).
\] Compute \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b\). Is it positive, negative, or zero? In one sentence, what does the sign tell you about how the two directions line up?

title: Lecture 04 — Inner product
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \(a=(4,1,2)\) and \(b=(1,0,1)\) be shopping lists (apples, bread, milk). Write \((a,b)\) and state its length.
Y2. Let \(c=(10,12,11,14,13)\) be five daily counts. Find \(c_{2:4}\).
Y3. Compute \((2,-1)^{\mathsf{T}}(3,4)\) and \((1,0)^{\mathsf{T}}(0,1)\).
Y4. A café tracks daily sales in the order (espresso, milk, syrup): \[
x = (40,\ 30,\ 10),
\] with prices in dollars \[
p = (3,\ 2,\ 1).
\] What quantity does \(p^{\mathsf{T}}x\) represent? Compute it.
Y5. Two shopping lists, in the order (apples, bread, milk): \[
r = (2,\ 1,\ 3), \qquad s = (4,\ 2,\ 6).
\] Compute \(r^{\mathsf{T}}s\). Notice anything about \(r\) and \(s\)? If \(t=(1,0,-1)\), compute \(r^{\mathsf{T}}t\) and say whether \(r\) and \(t\) are orthogonal.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \((a,b)=(4,1,2,1,0,1)\); length \(6\).
Y2. \(c_{2:4}=(12,11,14)\).
Y3. \((2,-1)^{\mathsf{T}}(3,4)=2\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot 4=2\). \((1,0)^{\mathsf{T}}(0,1)=0\) (orthogonal).
Y4. Total revenue in dollars: \(p^{\mathsf{T}}x=3\cdot 40+2\cdot 30+1\cdot 10=120+60+10=190\) dollars.
Y5. \(r^{\mathsf{T}}s=2\cdot 4+1\cdot 2+3\cdot 6=8+2+18=28\). Also \(s=2r\), so the lists are proportional (same “direction” in data space). \(r^{\mathsf{T}}t=2\cdot 1+1\cdot 0+3\cdot(-1)=2-3=-1\neq 0\), so \(r\) and \(t\) are not orthogonal.

title: Lecture 06 — Linear functions in applications
text:

Is \(f(x)=5x_1+2x_2\) linear, affine, or both? What about \(g(x)=5x_1+2x_2-3\)?

title: Lecture 06 — Linear functions in applications
text:
Fill in
An affine model \(f(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) often approximates a real quantity only over a limited range of inputs; outside that range the model may be \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
In a cost model \(c^{\mathsf{T}}q\), the entry \(c_i\) is the cost per unit of material \(i\). The total cost is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) of the amounts \(q_i\).
In Boyd 1.14, \(f^{\mathsf{T}}h\) is sector exposure: net dollars invested in assets with \(f_i=1\). If \(f^{\mathsf{T}}h=0\), the portfolio is \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) to that sector.
To pick the cheapest of \(K\) suppliers with price vectors \(p_1,\ldots,p_K\) for order \(q\), compare \(p_1^{\mathsf{T}}q,\ldots,p_K^{\mathsf{T}}q\) and choose the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
A regression model \(\hat{y}=\beta^{\mathsf{T}}x+v\) is useful when the relationship is roughly \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) over the data range, but coefficients can be hard to interpret if features are \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).

title: Lecture 06 — Linear functions in applications
text:
Worked in class
W1. A 30-question magazine quiz uses answers \(a_i\in\{1,2,3\}\) (Rarely, Sometimes, Often). Questions 1–15: Sometimes \(+1\), Often \(+2\). Questions 16–30: Sometimes \(+2\), Often \(+4\). Rarely adds 0. Write total score \(s=w^{\mathsf{T}}a+v\) (Boyd 2.6).
W2. Cash held in five currencies is \(c=(1000,500,-200,0,300)\) (USD, RMB, EUR, GBP, JPY). Exchange rates to USD are \(r=(1,0.14,1.08,1.27,0.0067)\). Total USD value is \(r^{\mathsf{T}}c\) (Boyd 1.12). Compute it (negative EUR is a liability).
W3. Three assets; pharma indicator \(f=(1,0,1)\). Portfolio \(h=(500,200,-100)\) dollars (short on asset 2). Compute exposure \(f^{\mathsf{T}}h\) (Boyd 1.14). In words, what does the sign mean?
W4. Order \(q=(10,5,20)\) of three materials. Supplier A prices \(p_A=(2,4,1)\); supplier B prices \(p_B=(3,2,2)\) per unit (Boyd 1.15). Which supplier is cheaper for the whole order? Compare \(p_A^{\mathsf{T}}q\) and \(p_B^{\mathsf{T}}q\).
W5. Processor temperature is affine in power: \(T=a^{\mathsf{T}}P+b\). Idle \(P=(10,10,10)\) gives \(T=30\). Full power on processor 1 only, \(P=(100,10,10)\), gives \(T=60\). Find \(a_1\) from those two readings (Boyd 2.2 setup).

title: Lecture 06 — Linear functions in applications
text:
Check yourself
C1. Two regression models for the same house: \(\hat{y}_A=200{,}000+120x_1+15{,}000x_2\) and \(\hat{y}_B=180{,}000+130x_1+18{,}000x_2\), where \(x_1\) is area (1000 ft²) and \(x_2\) is bedrooms. For \(x=(2,3)\), compute both predictions. Which predicts higher?
C2. Boyd 2.4 style: \(\varphi(1,1,0)=-1\), \(\varphi(-1,1,1)=1\), \(\varphi(1,-1,-1)=1\). Could \(\varphi\) be linear? Could it be affine? Brief reason.
C3. You must buy \(q=(4,2)\). Supplier 1: \(p_1=(5,3)\); supplier 2: \(p_2=(4,5)\). Which supplier wins on total cost \(p_k^{\mathsf{T}}q\)?
C4. A long-only portfolio (\(h_i\geq 0\)) is neutral to pharma (\(f^{\mathsf{T}}h=0\) with \(f_i\in\{0,1\}\)). In one sentence, what does that mean about pharma holdings?
C5. Name one reasonable limitation of using a linear model for café revenue \(p^{\mathsf{T}}x\) when \(x\) counts drinks sold.






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. \(\hat{y}_A=200{,}000+120\cdot 2+15{,}000\cdot 3=245{,}240\). \(\hat{y}_B=180{,}000+130\cdot 2+18{,}000\cdot 3=248{,}260\). Model B predicts higher.
C2. Cannot be linear: if \(\varphi(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x\), the three given values force an inconsistent system for \(a\). Could be affine: many choices of \(a,b\) with \(\varphi(x)=a^{\mathsf{T}}x+b\) fit three input–output pairs.
C3. \(p_1^{\mathsf{T}}q=5\cdot 4+3\cdot 2=26\). \(p_2^{\mathsf{T}}q=4\cdot 4+5\cdot 2=26\). Tie.
C4. No net dollar holdings in pharma stocks (long positions in pharma are fully offset by non-pharma or the portfolio holds none).
C5. Sample: prices fixed but demand may saturate; loss leaders; does not model quantity discounts; assumes all drinks sold at listed price.

title: Lecture 08 — Angle and similarity
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compute cosine similarity or an angle between vectors.
Distinguish closeness in position from similarity in direction.
Choose an appropriate similarity measure for a stated purpose.
Explain why normalization may change a comparison.

title: Lecture 08 — Angle and similarity
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,0)\) and \(b=(1,1)\).

Compute \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b\), \(\lVert a\rVert\), and \(\lVert b\rVert\).
Without finding the angle in degrees, is \(\cos\theta = a^{\mathsf{T}}b/(\lVert a\rVert\lVert b\rVert)\) closer to \(1\), to \(0\), or to \(-1\)? What does that suggest about the directions?

title: Lecture 08 — Angle and similarity
text:
Fill in
For nonzero \(n\)-vectors \(a\) and \(b\), the angle \(\theta=\angle(a,b)\) satisfies \[
\cos\theta = \frac{a^{\mathsf{T}}b}{\lVert a\rVert\,\lVert b\rVert}, \qquad \theta\in[0,\pi].
\] The quantity \(\dfrac{a^{\mathsf{T}}b}{\lVert a\rVert\,\lVert b\rVert}\) is the cosine similarity.
Cauchy–Schwarz says \(|a^{\mathsf{T}}b|\leq\lVert a\rVert\lVert b\rVert\), so the cosine is always between \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) and \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\).
Interpretation: - \(\theta\approx 0\) (cosine near \(1\)): directions nearly the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) - \(\theta=\pi/2\) (cosine \(0\)): vectors are \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) - \(\theta\approx\pi\) (cosine near \(-1\)): directions nearly \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\)
Distance \(\lVert a-b\rVert\) measures closeness of positions. Angle measures similarity of directions (independent of overall scale of each vector). Scaling \(a\) by a positive constant does \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) change \(\angle(a,b)\).
A normalized (unit) vector is \(\hat{a}=a/\lVert a\rVert\), which has \(\lVert\hat{a}\rVert=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\). Among unit vectors, smaller distance is equivalent to \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) angle (Boyd 3.24(b)).

title: Lecture 08 — Angle and similarity
text:
Software
Octave:
a = [1; 0]; b = [1; 1];
cos_th = (a'*b)/(norm(a)*norm(b))
th_deg = acosd(cos_th)    % angle in degrees
Python:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1.0, 0.0]); b = np.array([1.0, 1.0])
cos_th = (a @ b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
th_deg = np.degrees(np.arccos(np.clip(cos_th, -1, 1)))

title: Lecture 08 — Angle and similarity
text:
Worked in class
W1. Compute the cosine and the angle (degrees is fine) between \(u=(2,0)\) and \(v=(1,1)\). Sketch both from the origin.
W2. Distance vs direction. Let \(p=(1,1)\), \(q=(10,10)\), and \(r=(1,-1)\).

Compute \(\lVert p-q\rVert\) and \(\lVert p-r\rVert\). Which is closer in distance to \(p\)?
Compute \(\angle(p,q)\) and \(\angle(p,r)\). Which is more similar in direction to \(p\)?
In one sentence: when would you prefer angle over Euclidean distance?

W3. Nonnegative vectors (Boyd 3.23). Let \(x=(2,1)\) and \(y=(0,3)\).

Compute \(x^{\mathsf{T}}y\). Why must the angle be between \(0^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\)?
When are two nonzero nonnegative vectors orthogonal?

W4. Distance nearest neighbor vs angle nearest neighbor (Boyd 3.24(a)). Let \[
x=(1,0),\qquad z_1=(2,0),\qquad z_2=(0.5,0.5).
\] Find the distance nearest neighbor of \(x\) among \(\{z_1,z_2\}\) and the angle nearest neighbor. Are they the same?
W5. Normalization. Replace \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) by their unit versions \(\hat{z}_1=z_1/\lVert z_1\rVert\) and \(\hat{z}_2=z_2/\lVert z_2\rVert\). Does distance-NN of \(x\) among the unit vectors match angle-NN? (Boyd 3.24(b) idea.)

title: Lecture 08 — Angle and similarity
text:
Check yourself
C1. Cosine of the angle between \((3,4)\) and \((4,-3)\). Are they orthogonal?
C2. True or false: if \(\lVert a-b\rVert\) is small, then \(\angle(a,b)\) must be near \(0\). One counterexample or reason.
C3. Document word-count vectors (nonnegative). Why is angle a common similarity for documents?
C4. Octave or Python: write one line that prints the cosine similarity of a and b (assume they already exist).
C5. You normalize every candidate before using Euclidean distance to a query. What comparison are you effectively making?






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. \(a^{\mathsf{T}}b=12-12=0\), so cosine \(=0\). Yes, orthogonal (\(90^\circ\)).
C2. False. Example: \(a=(100,0)\), \(b=(101,0)\) are close in distance but that alone does not force a general claim for arbitrary nearby pairs that point opposite ways after a shift; clearer counterexample for “small distance \(\Rightarrow\) small angle”: take \(a=(0.01,0)\) and \(b=(-0.01,0)\) — distance \(0.02\) is small, but angle is \(180^\circ\).
C3. Documents can have very different lengths (total word counts). Angle / cosine ignores overall scale and focuses on the pattern of which words appear together.
C4. Octave: (a'*b)/(norm(a)*norm(b)). Python: (a @ b)/(np.linalg.norm(a)*np.linalg.norm(b)).
C5. Angle nearest-neighbor (among those candidates): after normalizing, Euclidean nearest matches smallest angle.

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Explain the goal of clustering.
Compute one assignment/update iteration of \(k\)-means.
Interpret a centroid as a vector.
Recognize that clustering output depends on representation, scaling, and initialization.

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:
Warm-up
Six points in \(\mathbb{R}^2\): \[
(0,0),\ (0,1),\ (1,0),\quad (5,5),\ (5,6),\ (6,5).
\] By eye, into how many natural groups do they fall? Suggest a representative (center) for each group.

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:
Fill in
Clustering partitions \(N\) vectors \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\) into \(k\) groups so that vectors in the same group are \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) to each other (small pairwise distances).
A group representative (centroid, when we use the mean) \(z_j\) is a vector that stands for cluster \(j\). The basic clustering objective sums squared distances from each point to its group’s representative: \[
J^{\mathrm{clust}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \lVert x_i - z_{c_i}\rVert^2,
\] where \(c_i\) is the cluster index of \(x_i\).
\(k\)-means alternates two steps:

Assignment: given representatives \(z_1,\ldots,z_k\), set each \(c_i\) to the index of the \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) \(z_j\) to \(x_i\).
Update: given assignments, replace each \(z_j\) by the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of the points currently in cluster \(j\).

The algorithm is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\): different initial \(z_j\) can yield different final clusterings. Feature \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) and the choice of \(k\) also change the result.

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:
Worked in class
W1. Goal in words. A café has purchase vectors (coffee, tea, pastry counts) for many customers. What would clustering these vectors help the café do?
W2. One assignment step. Data: \[
x_1=(0,0),\ x_2=(0,2),\ x_3=(8,0),\ x_4=(8,2).
\] Representatives \(z_1=(1,1)\), \(z_2=(7,1)\). Assign each \(x_i\) to the nearest \(z_j\). List the two clusters.
W3. One update step. Using your clusters from W2, replace each \(z_j\) by the mean of its points. What are the new centroids?
W4. Interpret a centroid. If a cluster of temperature vectors has centroid \((54,53,55)\) for three morning hours, what does that vector mean?
W5. Sensitivity. Same four points as W2, but start with \(z_1=(0,1)\), \(z_2=(0,0)\). After one assignment, what goes wrong if both points near the origin grab almost everything? (One sentence on initialization.)

title: Lecture 10 — Clustering and \(k\)-means
text:
Check yourself
C1. In \(k\)-means assignment, each point is assigned by a \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) computation to the current representatives.
C2. For points \((0,0),(2,0)\) in one cluster, the centroid is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
C3. True or false: running \(k\)-means once always finds the global minimum of \(J^{\mathrm{clust}}\).
C4. Why might you standardize features before clustering customer data that mixes age and annual spending?
C5. If \(k=N\) (one cluster per point), what is \(J^{\mathrm{clust}}\) after a perfect fit of representatives?






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. nearest-neighbor (distance to each representative)
C2. \((1,0)\)
C3. False. It is a heuristic; different initializations can give different local solutions.
C4. So spending in dollars does not dominate age in years inside Euclidean distance.
C5. \(J^{\mathrm{clust}}=0\) (each point is its own representative).

text:

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Recognize simple dependent and independent collections.
Construct a dependence relationship.
Interpret dependence as redundant information.
Explain why redundancy matters in data, measurement, and computation.

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,0)\), \(b=(0,1)\), and \(c=(1,1)\).

Find scalars \(\alpha,\beta\) (not both zero is fine) so that \(c=\alpha a+\beta b\).
In one sentence: is knowing \(c\) “new information” once you already know \(a\) and \(b\)?

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Fill in
A list of \(n\)-vectors \(a_1,\ldots,a_k\) is linearly dependent if there exist scalars \(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_k\), not all zero, such that \[
\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k = \underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}.
\] Any such nontrivial combination equal to zero is a dependence relation.
The list is linearly independent if the only solution of \(\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k=0\) is \(\beta_1=\cdots=\beta_k=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
Equivalent picture: the list is dependent if (and only if) at least one vector is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) of the others (or the list contains the zero vector).
Redundancy: if the vectors are features, sensors, or columns of data and they are dependent, then at least one measurement can be \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) from the others — it does not add a new independent piece of information.
A single nonzero vector is always \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\). Two vectors are dependent iff one is a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of the other.

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Worked in class
W1. Independent or dependent? For each list in \(\mathbb{R}^2\), decide and give a one-line reason.

\((1,0),\ (0,1)\)
\((2,4),\ (1,2)\)
\((1,1),\ (1,-1),\ (0,2)\)

W2. Construct a dependence relation. For \(u=(1,2)\), \(v=(2,1)\), \(w=(3,3)\), find \(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3\) not all zero with \(\beta_1 u+\beta_2 v+\beta_3 w=0\). (Hint: notice \(w=u+v\).)
W3. Sensors. Three temperature sensors report daily averages as vectors of length \(7\). Sensor C always equals (Sensor A \(+\) Sensor B)\(/2\). Are the three weekly report vectors dependent? What does that mean for “how many independent sensors” you really have?
W4. Features. Customer vectors (age, income, spending). Someone adds a fourth feature “age in months” \(=12\times\) age. Does the new feature add independent information for linear models that use these coordinates?
W5. Zero vector. Why is any list that includes \(0\) automatically dependent?

title: Lecture 12 — Linear dependence as redundancy
text:
Check yourself
C1. Are \((1,0,0)\), \((0,1,0)\), \((0,0,1)\) independent in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)? Brief reason.
C2. Find a dependence relation for \((1,1)\), \((2,2)\), \((0,1)\).
C3. True or false: if every pair in a list of three vectors is independent, then the whole list is independent.
C4. In one sentence: why might redundant features waste storage or confuse nearest-neighbor distance?
C5. Give one independent list of two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) and one dependent list of two vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^2\).






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. Yes. If \(\beta_1(1,0,0)+\beta_2(0,1,0)+\beta_3(0,0,1)=0\), then \((\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3)=0\), so only the trivial combination works.
C2. Example: \((1,1)\) and \((2,2)\) are multiples, so \(2\cdot(1,1)+(-1)\cdot(2,2)+0\cdot(0,1)=0\). (Any nontrivial relation that uses that fact is fine.)
C3. False. Counterexample: \((1,0)\), \((0,1)\), \((1,1)\) — each pair is independent, but the three are dependent because \((1,1)=(1,0)+(0,1)\).
C4. A redundant coordinate can overweight that direction in Euclidean distance (or store duplicated information) without adding a new independent signal.
C5. Independent example: \((1,0),\ (0,1)\). Dependent example: \((1,2),\ (2,4)\).

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Explain what a basis accomplishes.
Identify a basis and dimension in simple examples.
Use linear combination, span, subspace, independence, basis, and dimension accurately.
Recognize an orthonormal collection.
Explain why orthonormal coordinates are convenient for measurement and reconstruction.

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,0)\) and \(b=(1,1)\).

Is \(\{a,b\}\) independent? Does it span \(\mathbb{R}^2\)?
Can every \(v=(v_1,v_2)\) be written uniquely as \(\alpha a+\beta b\)? (Try \(v=(2,3)\).)

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Fill in
A basis of a subspace \(V\) is a list of vectors that is both

\(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) (no redundancy), and
a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) set for \(V\) (every vector in \(V\) is a linear combination of the list).

What a basis accomplishes: every \(v\in V\) has coefficients (coordinates) with respect to the basis — a unique recipe \(v=\beta_1 a_1+\cdots+\beta_k a_k\).
The dimension of \(V\) is the number of vectors in \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) of \(V\). (All bases of \(V\) have the same length.)
Examples:

\(\dim\mathbb{R}^n=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) (standard basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\)).
A line through the origin through a nonzero \(a\) has dimension \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
A plane through the origin spanned by two independent vectors has dimension \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).

An orthonormal list \(q_1,\ldots,q_k\) satisfies \(q_i^{\mathsf{T}}q_j=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) if \(i\neq j\), and \(\lVert q_i\rVert=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
For an orthonormal basis of a subspace, the coefficients of \(v\) are especially simple: \[
\beta_i = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}
\] (inner products — no linear system to solve). That is why orthonormal coordinates are convenient for measurement and reconstruction.

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Worked in class
W1. Basis or not? For each list, is it a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^2\)? If not, say whether it fails independence, spanning, or both.

\((1,0),\ (0,1)\)
\((1,1),\ (2,2)\)
\((1,0),\ (0,1),\ (1,1)\)
\((1,1)\) alone

W2. Dimension. Let \(V=\operatorname{span}\{(1,2,0),(2,4,0),(0,0,1)\}\). Find a basis of \(V\) and \(\dim V\).
W3. Vocabulary drill. Fill each blank with one of: linear combination, span, subspace, independent, dependent, basis, dimension.

\(\operatorname{span}\{a,b\}\) is always a \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
If \(c=2a-b\), then \(\{a,b,c\}\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
A \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(V\) is an independent spanning list for \(V\).

W4. Orthonormal check. Which of these pairs in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) is orthonormal?

\((1,0),\ (0,1)\)
\((1,1)/\sqrt{2},\ (1,-1)/\sqrt{2}\)
\((1,0),\ (1,1)\)

W5. Orthonormal coordinates. Let \(q_1=(1,0)\) and \(q_2=(0,1)\) (standard basis — already orthonormal). For \(v=(3,-2)\), what are \(\beta_1=q_1^{\mathsf{T}}v\) and \(\beta_2=q_2^{\mathsf{T}}v\)? Check \(v=\beta_1 q_1+\beta_2 q_2\).
W6 (time permitting). Gram–Schmidt idea. From independent \(a_1=(1,1)\) and \(a_2=(1,0)\), form \(q_1=a_1/\lVert a_1\rVert\), then subtract from \(a_2\) its projection onto \(q_1\), and normalize. (Board sketch only.)

title: Lecture 14 — Basis, dimension, and orthonormal vectors
text:
Check yourself
C1. A basis of a subspace is a list that is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) and \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
C2. \(\dim\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0)\}=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
C3. True or false: every spanning list for \(V\) is a basis of \(V\).
C4. If \(\{q_1,q_2\}\) is orthonormal and \(v=\beta_1 q_1+\beta_2 q_2\), then \(\beta_1=\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
C5. Why are orthonormal coordinates nicer than coordinates in a skewed basis like \((1,0),\ (1,1)\)?






NoteAnswers (Check yourself only)





C1. independent and spanning (for that subspace).
C2. \(2\)
C3. False. Spanning lists can be dependent (too many vectors); a basis cannot.
C4. \(\beta_1=q_1^{\mathsf{T}}v\)
C5. Coefficients are inner products (no \(2\times 2\) solve); lengths and angles stay easy because the basis vectors are unit and orthogonal.

title: Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Represent datasets, networks, images, or systems as matrices.
Perform matrix addition, scaling, and transposition.
Recognize zero, identity, diagonal, triangular, symmetric, and sparse matrices.
Explain one practical consequence of matrix structure.

title: Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A =
\begin{bmatrix}
2 & -1 & 0 \\
4 & 3 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

What are the dimensions of \(A\)? Is it tall, wide, or square?
What is \(A_{23}\)? What is the second column of \(A\) as a vector?

title: Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects
text:
Fill in
An \(m\times n\) matrix is a rectangular array with \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\) rows and \(\underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}\) columns. The entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is written \(A_{ij}\) (Boyd: indices start at \(1\)).
We can view \(A\) as its \(n\) columns (each an \(m\)-vector) side by side, or as its \(m\) rows (each an \(n\)-row-vector) stacked.
Examples of “matrix as data”:

An image: pixel values in a grid.
A table: locations \(\times\) days, or customers \(\times\) products.
A relation / directed graph: adjacency matrix with \(A_{ij}=1\) when there is an edge from \(j\) to \(i\) (Boyd’s convention).

Transpose. \((A^{\mathsf{T}})_{ij}=\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\). If \(A\) is \(m\times n\), then \(A^{\mathsf{T}}\) is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
Addition and scaling. \(A+B\) and \(\beta A\) are entrywise (same size required for addition).
Special matrices (square, unless noted):



Name
Pattern




Zero \(0\)
all entries \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\)


Identity \(I\)
\(1\)s on the diagonal, \(0\)s elsewhere


Diagonal
off-diagonal entries are \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\)


Upper triangular
zeros \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) the diagonal


Symmetric
\(A^{\mathsf{T}}=\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\)


Sparse
\(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) of the entries are nonzero



Practical consequence: structure (sparsity, triangularity, symmetry) often means cheaper storage or faster algorithms — we take advantage of the pattern instead of treating every entry as generic.

title: Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects
text:
Worked in class
W1. Dimensions and pieces. Let \[
B =
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & -2 \\
3 & 4 & 5 \\
0 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Give \(B_{31}\), the third row, and the first column. Is \(B\) square?
W2. Data matrix. Three weather stations record (high °F, low °F) for one day. Station 1: \((62,48)\); station 2: \((58,45)\); station 3: \((65,50)\). Write a \(2\times 3\) matrix \(W\) whose columns are the station readings. What does \(W_{12}\) mean?
W3. Arithmetic. With \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{bmatrix},\quad
C=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\3&2\end{bmatrix},
\] compute \(A+C\), \(2A\), and \(A^{\mathsf{T}}\).
W4. Structure check. For each matrix, name every special type that applies (zero / identity / diagonal / triangular / symmetric / sparse — sparse is judgment call for tiny examples).

\(\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&-3\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}1&4\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{bmatrix}\)

W5. Why structure matters. An \(n\times n\) identity matrix has how many nonzero entries? Density \(nnz/(n^2)\)? Why might software store only the nonzeros of a sparse customer-purchase matrix?

title: Lecture 18 — Matrices as data and structured objects
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
M =
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 2 & 1 \\
-1 & 3 & 4
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Dimensions? \(M_{21}\)? Second column? Is \(M\) tall or wide?
Y2. A tiny directed graph on nodes \(\{1,2,3\}\) has edges \(2\to 1\), \(1\to 3\), and \(3\to 2\). Using Boyd’s convention (\(A_{ij}=1\) means edge from \(j\) to \(i\)), write the \(3\times 3\) adjacency matrix.
Y3. With \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&3\end{bmatrix}\), compute \(A+A^{\mathsf{T}}\). Is the result symmetric? Why?
Y4. True or false, with a one-line reason: every diagonal matrix is symmetric.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(2\times 3\); wide. \(M_{21}=-1\). Second column \((2,3)\).
Y2. \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 \\
1 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\] (edge \(2\to 1\) puts a \(1\) in row 1, column 2; \(1\to 3\) puts a \(1\) in row 3, column 1; \(3\to 2\) puts a \(1\) in row 2, column 3).
Y3. \(A+A^{\mathsf{T}}=\begin{bmatrix}2&2\\2&6\end{bmatrix}\), which equals its transpose, so yes — sum of a matrix and its transpose is always symmetric.
Y4. True. Off-diagonal entries are already \(0=0\), so \(A^{\mathsf{T}}=A\).

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Predict the effect of scaling, reflection, shear, and rotation matrices.
Apply matrices to many 2D or 3D points at once.
Plot and compare original and transformed objects.
Adapt a short program that implements a transformation.
Interpret a matrix as a coordinate or physical-space transformation.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Warm-up
Predict, without multiplying: where does \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1/2)\) send the point \((1,1)\)? Sketch the original and image roughly.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Fill in
Many geometric maps on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) (or \(\mathbb{R}^3\)) are matrix-vector products \(y=Ax\).
Finding the matrix. The \(j\)th column of \(A\) is what the map does to \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\). So apply the geometry to \(e_1,e_2\) (and \(e_3\) in 3D) to read off columns.
Common \(2\times 2\) examples:

Scaling / dilation: \(A=\operatorname{diag}(s_1,s_2)\) stretches the axes by \(s_1,s_2\).
Rotation counterclockwise by \(\theta\): \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Reflection through a line through the origin; shear (e.g. \(\begin{bmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\)).

Many points at once. If columns of \(X\) are points, then \(AX\) applies the same map to every column.
Change of coordinates (3D idea). Body-fixed vs earth-fixed frames: \(x_{\mathrm{earth}}=p+Qx_{\mathrm{body}}\), where columns of \(Q\) are the body axes expressed in earth coordinates.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Worked in class
W1. Build from \(e_1,e_2\). Reflection through the \(x_1\)-axis sends \((1,0)\mapsto(1,0)\) and \((0,1)\mapsto(0,-1)\). Write \(A\). Check \(A(2,3)\).
W2. Rotation. For \(\theta=90^\circ=\pi/2\), write the rotation matrix and compute \(A(1,0)\) and \(A(0,1)\). Does that match “\(90^\circ\) counterclockwise”?
W3. Many points. Let \(X=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&1\\0&1&1\end{bmatrix}\) (three corners of a right triangle). With \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\), compute \(AX\) and describe the image.
W4 (time permitting). Shear \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). Where do \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) go? Sketch the unit square’s image.

title: Lecture 20 — Transforming space
text:
Your turn
Y1. Reflection through the \(x_2\)-axis: write \(A\) by tracking \(e_1\) and \(e_2\), then compute \(A(3,-1)\).
Y2. Rotation by \(180^\circ\): write \(A\) and apply it to \((2,1)\).
Y3. True or false: every \(2\times 2\) matrix represents a rotation of the plane.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(e_1\mapsto(-1,0)\), \(e_2\mapsto(0,1)\), so \(A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). \(A(3,-1)=(-3,-1)\).
Y2. \(A=\begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}=-I\). \(A(2,1)=(-2,-1)\).
Y3. False. Scaling, shear, projections, and many other maps are also \(2\times 2\) matrices; rotations are a special family.

title: Lecture 22 — RREF and linear dynamical systems
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Read a reduced row echelon form: name pivot and free variables and write a parametric solution.
Tell inconsistent, unique, and infinitely many solutions apart from that form.
Write an evolving system as \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) and build the transition matrix from a flow description.
Compute and interpret the next state or two.

Checking a software solve with the residual \(Ax-b\) is mentioned below and practiced in Lab 2 and Lab 3. Many time steps, plots, and long-run patterns wait for the simulation lecture.

title: Lecture 22 — RREF and linear dynamical systems
text:
Warm-up
The RREF of an augmented matrix is \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 2 & | & 3 \\
0 & 1 & -1 & | & 4 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & | & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Which variables are pivots? Which are free? Write the general solution.

title: Lecture 22 — RREF and linear dynamical systems
text:
Fill in
Reduced row echelon form (RREF) is echelon form with these extras:

Each pivot is \(\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\).
Each pivot is the \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) nonzero in its column (zeros above and below).

A pivot variable corresponds to a pivot column. A free variable has \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) pivot in its column; assign a parameter (for example \(x_3=t\)).
Reading the RREF of \([A\mid b]\):







Pattern
Conclusion




A row \([0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c]\) with \(c\neq 0\)
\(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\)


Every column of \(A\) has a pivot, and the system is consistent
\(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) solution


Consistent, and at least one free variable
\(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) solutions



A row of zeros including the right-hand side is redundant, not inconsistent. Software can compute RREF or a solution (rref, A\b, numpy.linalg.solve). Verify a candidate \(x\) by the residual \(Ax-b\), which should be near \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\).
A linear dynamical system (discrete time) has the form \[
x_{t+1}=\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}},
\] where \(t=0,1,2,\ldots\) is the time index.

The state \(x_t\) is an \(n\)-vector that describes the system at time \(t\).
The matrix \(A\) is the transition matrix. Its size is \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\).

Columns. Column \(j\) of \(A\) is the next state if the current state is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\).
A few steps by hand. \(x_1=Ax_0\), \(x_2=Ax_1\), and so on. Packaging \(t\) steps as \(A^t\) comes later. To build \(A\) from a flow, ask: if everything starts in compartment \(j\), where does it go next? Those destinations are column \(j\).

title: Lecture 22 — RREF and linear dynamical systems
text:
Worked in class
W1. Classify from RREF. Unique, none, or infinitely many?

\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & | & 2 \\
0 & 1 & | & -1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & | & 3 \\
0 & 0 & | & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\]
\[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 & | & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & | & 4
\end{bmatrix}
\]

W2. Parametric form. From \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 3 & 0 & | & 2 \\
0 & 0 & 1 & | & -1
\end{bmatrix},
\] name the free variable and write \(x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)\) in terms of a parameter.
W3. Build a transition matrix. Two towns, Arcata and Eureka, exchange residents each year:

Of those in Arcata, \(80\%\) stay and \(20\%\) move to Eureka.
Of those in Eureka, \(90\%\) stay and \(10\%\) move to Arcata.

Order the state as \(x_t=(\text{Arcata},\text{Eureka})\). Write \(A\). With \(x_0=(5000,7000)\), compute \(x_1\). Does Arcata rise or fall in that year?
W4 (if time). State and matrix. A campus tracks (on-campus, off-campus) as \(x_t\) with \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.15\\ 0.3&0.85\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) What does \(A_{12}\) mean in words? (b) What does the first column represent? (c) If \(x_0=(800,200)\), compute \(x_1\) and interpret both entries as people.
W5 (if time). One residual. For \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix},\quad
b=\begin{bmatrix}5\\11\end{bmatrix},
\] solve \(Ax=b\) with Octave or Python and compute \(Ax-b\).

title: Lecture 22 — RREF and linear dynamical systems
text:
Your turn
Start with Y1–Y3 and Y5–Y6. The others are extra practice of the same skills.
Y1. From the RREF \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & -2 & | & 5 \\
0 & 1 & 3 & | & -1 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & | & 0
\end{bmatrix},
\] list pivot variables, free variables, and the general solution.
Y2. True or false: if RREF has a row of all zeros including the augmented entry, the system is inconsistent.
Y3. A \(3\times 5\) matrix \(A\), after a consistent RREF of \([A\mid b]\), has \(3\) pivots. How many free variables? Unique solution or infinitely many?
Y4. You solve \(Ax=b\) in software and get \(x=(1,-1)\). You compute \(Ax-b=(0.0,\,10^{-15})\). Was the solve successful? Why check the residual?
Y5. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\), then knowing \(x_t\) and \(A\) determines \(x_{t+1}\) uniquely.
Y6. Two warehouses, \(x_t=(\text{A},\text{B})\). Each day, A keeps \(70\%\) and ships \(30\%\) to B; B keeps \(60\%\) and ships \(40\%\) to A. Write \(A\). With \(x_0=(100,50)\), find \(x_1\).
Y7. With \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1.1&0\\0&0.5\end{bmatrix}\) and \(x_0=(2,8)\), compute \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). Which component is growing? Which is shrinking?
Y8 (if time). Three age groups (youth, adult, senior): \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
0.6 & 0 & 0 \\
0.4 & 0.7 & 0 \\
0 & 0.3 & 0.8
\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x_0=(100,200,50).
\] Interpret \(A_{21}\) and \(A_{33}\) in one phrase each, and compute \(x_1\).






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Pivot variables \(x_1,x_2\); free \(x_3=t\). Then \(x_1-2t=5\) and \(x_2+3t=-1\), so \[
x=(5+2t,\,-1-3t,\,t),\quad t\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Y2. False. A zero row including the right-hand side is consistent (a redundant equation). Inconsistency needs \([0\ \cdots\ 0\mid c]\) with \(c\neq 0\).
Y3. \(n=5\) unknowns and \(3\) pivots \(\Rightarrow\) \(2\) free variables \(\Rightarrow\) infinitely many solutions (when consistent).
Y4. Yes — the residual is numerically zero (roundoff). Checking \(Ax-b\) catches a wrong \(x\), a singular system, or a copy-paste mistake. Fuller software practice is Lab 3.
Y5. True. The rule \(x_{t+1}=Ax_t\) is a function of the current state: one matrix–vector product gives the unique next state.
Y6. \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}0.7&0.4\\ 0.3&0.6\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x_1=\begin{bmatrix}90\\60\end{bmatrix}.
\] Column 1: keep \(70\%\) in A and ship \(30\%\) to B. Column 2: ship \(40\%\) of B to A and keep \(60\%\) in B.
Y7. \(x_1=(2.2,4)\), \(x_2=(2.42,2)\). The first component grows (factor \(1.1\) each step); the second shrinks (factor \(0.5\)).
Y8. \(A_{21}=0.4\): the factor sending youth to adults in one step. \(A_{33}=0.8\): the factor of seniors who remain seniors. \[
x_1=Ax_0=\begin{bmatrix}60\\180\\100\end{bmatrix}.
\]

title: Lecture 24 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Determine whether a product is defined and give its dimensions.
Compute a small matrix product.
Interpret \(ABx\) as a sequence of transformations.
Explain why matrix multiplication is generally not commutative.

title: Lecture 24 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\3&2\end{bmatrix},\qquad
x=\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}.
\]

What are the dimensions of \(A\) and of \(B\)? Is \(AB\) defined? If so, what size is it?
Compute \(Bx\) (a \(2\)-vector). You will need this later as “\(B\) first, then \(A\).”

title: Lecture 24 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Fill in
If \(A\) is \(m\times n\) and \(B\) is \(n\times p\), the product \(AB\) is the \(m\times p\) matrix whose \(j\)th column is \[
(AB)_j = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}.
\] Equivalently, entry \((i,j)\) is the inner product of \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(A\) with \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) of \(B\): \[
(AB)_{ij} = a_i^{\mathsf{T}} b_j.
\]
When is \(AB\) defined? The inner dimensions must match: number of \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) of \(A\) equals number of \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) of \(B\).
Associativity (for vectors). For a compatible \(p\)-vector \(x\), \[
(AB)x = A(Bx).
\] Reading right to left: apply \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) first, then \(\underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\). So \(ABx\) is a sequence of transformations.
Not commutative. In general \(AB\neq BA\) (even when both products are defined). Order of maps matters: “rotate then reflect” is not the same as “reflect then rotate.”

title: Lecture 24 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Worked in class
W1. Dimensions. For each pair, decide whether \(AB\) is defined and give the size of \(AB\) if it is.

\(A\) is \(3\times 2\), \(B\) is \(2\times 4\).
\(A\) is \(2\times 3\), \(B\) is \(2\times 4\).
\(A\) is \(2\times 2\), \(B\) is \(2\times 2\).

W2. Compute a product. With \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&-1\end{bmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\3&2\end{bmatrix},
\] compute \(AB\) by forming columns \(Ab_1\) and \(Ab_2\) (or by row–column inner products).
W3. Sequence of maps. Using the same \(A\), \(B\), and \(x=(1,-1)\) from the warm-up, compute \(Bx\), then \(A(Bx)\). Compare with \((AB)x\) using your \(AB\) from W2. Same answer?
W4. Non-commutativity. With the same \(A\) and \(B\), compute \(BA\). Is \(BA=AB\)?

title: Lecture 24 — Matrix multiplication
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
C=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-1\\2&1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
D=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Is \(CD\) defined? Size? Compute \(CD\).
Y2. Is \(DC\) defined? If so, give its size (you need not compute every entry unless time allows). What does this say about “\(CD\) vs \(DC\)”?
Y3. Let \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (\(90^\circ\) CCW) and \(S=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\) (horizontal stretch). Compute \(RSx\) and \(SRx\) for \(x=(1,0)\). Same point? Interpret in one sentence.
Y4. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(AB\) and \(BA\) are both defined, then \(A\) and \(B\) must be square of the same size.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(C\) is \(2\times 3\), \(D\) is \(3\times 2\), so \(CD\) is defined and \(2\times 2\): \[
CD=\begin{bmatrix}-2&2\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.
\] (Columns: \(Cd_1=(-2,1)\), \(Cd_2=(2,2)\).)
Y2. Yes — \(D\) is \(3\times 2\) and \(C\) is \(2\times 3\), so \(DC\) is \(3\times 3\). Even when both products exist they need not have the same size, so they cannot be equal as matrices. Order matters.
Y3. \(Sx=(2,0)\), then \(RSx=(0,2)\). Meanwhile \(Rx=(0,1)\), then \(SRx=(0,1)\). Different: stretch-then-rotate \(\neq\) rotate-then-stretch for this \(x\).
Y4. False. Example: \(A\) is \(2\times 3\) and \(B\) is \(3\times 2\) — both \(AB\) (\(2\times 2\)) and \(BA\) (\(3\times 3\)) are defined, but neither factor is square. (They become the same size only when \(m=n\).)

title: Lecture 26 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:

title: Lecture 26 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compare algebraically equivalent orders of computation.
Count intermediate values that must be stored.
Measure runtime for increasing problem sizes.
Explain why forming a large intermediate matrix may be wasteful.
Choose a computational order and justify it quantitatively.

title: Lecture 26 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Warm-up
Let \(a=(1,2)\), \(b=(3,4)\), \(c=(1,-1)\) (column vectors).

Form the outer product \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) (a \(2\times 2\) matrix).
Compute \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) and \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\). Same vector?

title: Lecture 26 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Fill in
Associativity. For compatible sizes, \((XY)z=X(Yz)\). In particular, for \(n\)-vectors \(a,b,c\), \[
(ab^{\mathsf{T}})c = a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c).
\] Same mathematical result — different \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\).
Order 1 — form the matrix first. Compute \(M=ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) (\(n\times n\)), then \(Mc\).

Intermediate storage: about \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) numbers (the whole matrix \(M\)).
Cost idea: building \(M\) and multiplying by \(c\) scales like \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\) work (order \(n^2\)).

Order 2 — scalar first. Compute \(s=b^{\mathsf{T}}c\) (one number), then \(sa\).

Intermediate storage: the scalar \(s\), plus the vectors — order \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\) numbers, not \(n^2\).
Cost idea: two inner/scale passes — order \(\underline{\hspace{1.2cm}}\) work.

Why wasteful? Forming \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) materializes a dense \(n\times n\) matrix you may never need as an object; then you immediately collapse it with \(c\). Capstone theme: choose an algorithm that matches the structure, not only the formula on the page.
Runtime. In software you can time both orders for growing \(n\) and justify which order to use with measured times (and storage counts).

title: Lecture 26 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Worked in class
W1. Algebra. With \(a=(2,0,-1)\), \(b=(1,1,1)\), \(c=(1,0,1)\), compute \(s=b^{\mathsf{T}}c\) and \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\). Then form \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) and \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\). Match?
W2. Storage count. For general \(n\), how many entries does \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) have? How many numbers do you store for the scalar-first method beyond the three input vectors?
W3. Choose an order. You need \(y=(ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) for \(n=5000\) once. Which order do you run, and what two quantitative reasons (storage + flops/runtime idea) support the choice?
W4 (preview). Sketch what a timing table should look like: rows \(n=200,1000,3000\); columns “form \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\) then multiply” vs “scalar first.” What qualitative pattern do you expect?

title: Lecture 26 — Same mathematics, very different computational cost
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \(a=(1,-1,0)\), \(b=(2,1,3)\), \(c=(0,1,1)\). Compute both \((ab^{\mathsf{T}})c\) and \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)\).
Y2. For \(n=100\), about how many intermediate entries does Order 1 store in \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\)? Order 2 in the scalar \(s\)?
Y3. One sentence: why can two algebraically equal expressions have wildly different runtimes?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(b^{\mathsf{T}}c=2\cdot 0+1\cdot 1+3\cdot 1=4\), so \(a(b^{\mathsf{T}}c)=4a=(4,-4,0)\). The matrix route gives the same: \[
ab^{\mathsf{T}}=\begin{bmatrix}2&1&3\\-2&-1&-3\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad
(ab^{\mathsf{T}})c=(4,-4,0).
\]
Y2. Order 1 stores \(n^2=10{,}000\) entries in \(ab^{\mathsf{T}}\). Order 2 stores one scalar \(s\) as the essential intermediate (beyond the inputs).
Y3. Associativity preserves the value but not the work: different parenthesizations create different intermediates (e.g. an \(n\times n\) matrix vs a scalar), so flops and memory — and therefore runtime — can differ by orders of magnitude.

title: Lecture 28 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Interpret column space and null space through \(Ax=b\) and \(Ax=0\).
Determine rank from pivots or independent columns.
Find simple bases for column or null spaces.

title: Lecture 28 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
2 & 4 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Are the three columns independent? (Look carefully at columns 1 and 2.)
For which \(b\) can \(Ax=b\) have a solution — any \(b\) in \(\mathbb{R}^3\), or only some?

title: Lecture 28 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Fill in
The column space \(C(A)\) is the span of the columns of \(A\). Solving \(Ax=b\) asks: is \(b\) in \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\)?
The null space \(N(A)\) is the set of solutions of \(Ax=\underline{\hspace{0.8cm}}\). It always contains \(0\); nontrivial null vectors mean dependent columns.
A subspace is a nonempty set closed under addition and scaling. Both \(C(A)\) and \(N(A)\) are subspaces.
A basis is a linearly independent spanning set. The dimension of a subspace is the number of vectors in any basis.
The rank of \(A\) is \[
\operatorname{rank}(A) = \underline{\hspace{3.6cm}}
\] (equivalently: number of pivot columns after elimination / RREF). Then \[
\dim C(A)=\operatorname{rank}(A),\qquad \dim N(A)=n-\operatorname{rank}(A)
\] for an \(m\times n\) matrix (number of free variables \(=\) nullity).
Reading RREF for bases.

Pivot columns of the original \(A\) form a basis for \(C(A)\).
Free-variable special solutions form a basis for \(N(A)\).







NoteEnrichment (not on quizzes)



Strang’s other two subspaces: the row space \(C(A^{\mathsf{T}})\) and left nullspace \(N(A^{\mathsf{T}})\). Same rank story; we do not drill them for Quiz 10 / Midterm 2.

title: Lecture 28 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Worked in class
W1. Column space via \(Ax=b\). Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Describe \(C(A)\) in words. Is \(b=(1,2,3)\) in \(C(A)\)? Is \(b=(1,3,0)\)?
W2. Null space. Same \(A\). Solve \(Ax=0\). Give a basis for \(N(A)\) (it may be \(\{0\}\) only — say so).
W3. Rank from pivots. The RREF of \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 3 \\
2 & 4 & 6 \\
0 & 1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}
\] is \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 1 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] What is \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\)? Which columns of the original \(A\) form a basis for \(C(A)\)? Find a basis for \(N(A)\).
W4. Dictionary. Match each phrase to the right idea: consistency of \(Ax=b\); uniqueness of the solution when it exists; “how big is the column space?”

title: Lecture 28 — Rank, column space, null space, and basis connections
text:
Your turn
Y1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 \\
-1 & -2 \\
0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Find \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\) and a basis for \(C(A)\). Is \(b=(2,-2,0)\) in \(C(A)\)?
Y2. For the same \(A\), find a basis for \(N(A)\). How many free variables?
Y3. True or false: if \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\) for an \(m\times n\) matrix with \(m\ge n\), then \(Ax=0\) has only the zero solution.
Y4. True or false: row space and left nullspace will appear on Quiz 10.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Columns: \(a_2=2a_1\), so \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=1\). Basis for \(C(A)\): \(\{(1,-1,0)\}\) (or any nonzero multiple). Yes — \(b=2a_1\).
Y2. \(Ax=0\) means \(x_1+2x_2=0\), so \(x=(-2t,\,t)=t(-2,1)\). Basis for \(N(A)\): \(\{(-2,1)\}\). One free variable; \(\dim N(A)=1=2-\operatorname{rank}(A)\).
Y3. True. Full column rank means no free variables, so \(N(A)=\{0\}\).
Y4. False. Enrichment only — not quiz material.

title: Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Download PDF
Last updated: October 8, 2026.
Textbook: Boyd & Vandenberghe, VMLS (PDF)
Strang / MIT (optional): Reading: Strang §6.1 (PDF) — eigenvalues
Video: 18.06 Lec 21 — eigenvalues and eigenvectors · MIT 18.06 playlist (Strang)
Reading: Beginning of Strang §6.1 — \(Ax=\lambda x\), eigenvectors, and dynamics. Related objectives: Lectures. Schedule.
Bring paper. Warm-up while attendance is taken, then fill-in notes, board examples, and Your turn.
Callback: Lab 4 asked why \(B=\operatorname{diag}(1.2,\,0.5)\) grows from some starts and decays from others. Today we name the missing idea: eigenvectors.

title: Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Explain geometrically what makes \(v\) an eigenvector.
Verify a proposed eigenpair.
Find \(\lambda\) when an eigenvector is given.
Connect eigenvectors to repeated transformations and steady directions.
Recognize that a rotation may have no real eigenvector, motivating complex numbers.

title: Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Warm-up
Lab 4 mystery matrix: \[
B=\begin{bmatrix}1.2&0\\0&0.5\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Compute \(B\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(B\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}\). Is each output a scalar multiple of the input?
Starting from \(x_0=(1,0)\) vs \(y_0=(0,1)\), which trajectory grows and which decays? Why, in one sentence using part (a)?

title: Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Fill in
Eigenpair. A nonzero vector \(v\) is an eigenvector of square \(A\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\) if \[
Av = \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}.
\] Geometrically: \(A\) sends \(v\) to a vector on the \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) line through \(v\) (scaled by \(\lambda\); if \(\lambda<0\), also flipped).
Verify. Given a candidate pair \((\lambda,v)\), compute \(Av\) and \(\lambda v\); they must \(\underline{\hspace{1.6cm}}\).
Find \(\lambda\) from \(v\). If \(v\neq 0\) is known to be an eigenvector and some component \(v_i\neq 0\), then \[
\lambda = \frac{(Av)_i}{v_i}
\] (same ratio for every nonzero component).
Dynamics. If \(x_0=v\) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue \(\lambda\), then \[
x_t = A^t v = \underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}.
\] The direction of \(v\) is persistent: each step only rescales (and maybe flips). That is why Lab 4’s two axis starts behaved so differently.
No real eigenvector. A pure rotation (e.g. \(90^\circ\)) moves every real nonzero vector off its own line. Then there is \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) real eigenpair — we will need complex numbers on Wednesday.

title: Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Worked in class
W1. Geometry. Sketch \(v=(1,1)\) and \(Av\) for \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}\). Is \(v\) an eigenvector? What about \(e_1=(1,0)\)?
W2. Verify. Check whether \((\lambda,v)=(3,(1,1))\) is an eigenpair of \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}.
\] Compute both \(Av\) and \(\lambda v\).
W3. Find \(\lambda\). You are told that \(v=(1,-1)\) is an eigenvector of \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}4&2\\1&3\end{bmatrix}.
\] Find \(\lambda\). Then confirm \(Av=\lambda v\).
W4. Lab 4 explained. For \(B=\operatorname{diag}(1.2,\,0.5)\):

Name two real eigenpairs (use the standard basis).
If \(x_0=c_1 e_1+c_2 e_2\), what is \(x_t=B^t x_0\)? Which term dominates for large \(t\) when \(c_1\neq 0\)?

W5. Rotation. Let \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) (\(90^\circ\) CCW). For a generic \(v=(a,b)\neq 0\), is \(Rv\) a real multiple of \(v\)? What does that say about real eigenvectors of \(R\)?

title: Lecture 35 — Eigenvectors as persistent directions
text:
Your turn
Y1. Verify or reject: is \((\lambda,v)=(−1,(1,-1))\) an eigenpair of \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\)?
Y2. Given that \(v=(1,2)\) is an eigenvector of \(A=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\2&1\end{bmatrix}\), find \(\lambda\).
Y3. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(Av=2v\) and \(v\neq 0\), then \(A^3 v=8v\).
Y4. In one sentence: why did Lab 4’s diagonal mystery need eigenvectors (not just “look at the plot”)?






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(Av=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\-1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}\) and \((-1)v=\begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}\). Yes — eigenpair.
Y2. \(Av=\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\2&1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1\\2\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\4\end{bmatrix}\). Ratio from the first component: \(\lambda=3/1=3\). Check second: \(4=3\cdot 2\). So \(\lambda=3\).
Y3. True. \(A^3 v=A^2(Av)=A^2(2v)=A(4v)=8v\) (or \(A^t v=\lambda^t v\)).
Y4. Sample: The plot shows growth vs decay by start direction; eigenvectors name the persistent directions (and their growth factors \(\lambda\)) that explain why.

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a general matrix with software.
Verify \(Av\approx\lambda v\) numerically.
Use dominant eigenbehavior to explain a simulated system.
Interpret complex eigenvalues as rotation/oscillation behavior.
Explore a symmetric-matrix or normal-mode example and observe orthogonal eigenvectors.

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Warm-up
Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}1.1&0.2\\0.1&0.8\end{bmatrix},\qquad
v=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}.
\] Hand-compute \(Av\). Guess a plausible \(\lambda\) so that \(Av\approx\lambda v\). (Exact eigenpairs come from software in lab.)

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Fill in
Software eigenpairs. Octave eig(A) / Python np.linalg.eig(A) return eigenvalues and a matrix whose columns are eigenvectors.
Verify. For each reported pair \((\lambda,v)\), check \[
Av \approx \underline{\hspace{1.4cm}}
\] (componentwise; floating-point noise is expected). Never trust a bare printout without this check.
Dominant behavior. If \(|\lambda_1|>|\lambda_2|\ge\cdots\) and \(x_0\) has a component along the \(\lambda_1\)-eigenvector, then for large \(t\) \[
A^t x_0 \approx c\,\lambda_1^t\,v_1.
\] That explains Lab 4-style growth/decay/stabilization once you know the eigenpairs.
Complex eigenvalues. For a real matrix, nonreal eigenvalues come in conjugate pairs. In the real plane they produce \(\underline{\hspace{2.4cm}}\) (rotation / oscillation), matching Monday’s pure-rotation example.
Normal modes (demo, not a DE course). For a symmetric mass–spring style matrix, eigenvectors are often \(\underline{\hspace{2.0cm}}\) (orthogonal). Software shows the modes; we do not derive differential equations today.

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Worked in class
W1. Software sketch. On the board / laptop, for \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\):
# Octave:  [V,D] = eig(A)     or    eig(A)
# Python:  vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
Read off \(\lambda\)’s and columns of \(V\). Verify \(A v_1=\lambda_1 v_1\) for one column.
W2. Explain a simulation. Same \(A\) as W1; \(x_0=(1,0)\). Using eigenpairs, explain in one sentence why \(x_t\) grows and which direction it approaches.
W3. Complex / oscillation. Software on \(R=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\) should report eigenvalues near \(\pm i\). Connect that to the cycling you saw in Lab 4 stretch / Lecture 35.
W4. Symmetric demo. Let \(S=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\) (symmetric). Check that the two eigenvectors from W1 are orthogonal (\(v_1^{\mathsf{T}}v_2=0\)). Normal-mode pictures use the same idea in higher dimension.

title: Lecture 37 — Why did the system behave that way?
text:
Your turn
Y1. Pseudocode: given \(A\), obtain eigenpairs in software and write the one-line check that \(Av\approx\lambda v\) for the first pair.
Y2. True or false: if \(|\lambda_1|=1.5\) and \(|\lambda_2|=0.5\), then for generic \(x_0\) the long-run direction of \(A^t x_0\) is the \(\lambda_1\)-eigendirection.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. Sample: vals, V = np.linalg.eig(A) then A @ V[:,0] - vals[0]*V[:,0] (should be near \(0\)); Octave: [V,D]=eig(A) then A*V(:,1) - D(1,1)*V(:,1).
Y2. True. The \(\lambda_1\) term grows relative to \(\lambda_2\), so the state aligns with \(v_1\) (unless the \(v_1\)-component of \(x_0\) is exactly zero).

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Learning objectives
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Compute a least-squares solution with Octave or Python.
Plot observed and fitted values.
Interpret residuals and an RMS error in context.
Check the residual’s orthogonality to the columns of \(A\).
Evaluate whether a fitted model is useful rather than merely reporting coefficients.
Recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is symmetric positive semidefinite, explain \(x^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax=\lVert Ax\rVert^2\), and recognize that \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is positive definite when \(A\) has linearly independent columns.

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Warm-up
Monday’s setup: minimize \(\|Ax-b\|\). At a minimizer \(\hat{x}\), the residual \(r=b-A\hat{x}\) is orthogonal to \(C(A)\), which is equivalent to the normal equations \[
A^{\mathsf{T}}A\,\hat{x}=A^{\mathsf{T}}b.
\]

If \(A\) is \(m\times n\) with \(m>n\), what size is \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\)? Why is that nicer than solving \(Ax=b\) directly?
True or false: \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always symmetric.

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Fill in
Normal equations / software. Solving \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\hat{x}=A^{\mathsf{T}}b\) (when \(A\) has independent columns) gives the unique least-squares \(\hat{x}\). In practice we often call a solver instead of forming \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) by hand:








Task
Octave
Python




Least-squares \(\hat{x}\)
xhat = A \ b
xhat = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0]


Fitted values
bhat = A*xhat
bhat = A @ xhat


Residual
r = b - bhat
r = b - bhat


RMS
rms = norm(r)/sqrt(m)
rms = np.linalg.norm(r)/np.sqrt(m)



Orthogonality check. At a least-squares solution, \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r \approx \underline{\hspace{1.0cm}}\) (numerical noise ok).
RMS. Root-mean-square residual \(\mathrm{RMS}=\|r\|/\sqrt{m}\) reports a typical per-equation error in the same units as \(b\).
Useful vs coefficients. Always ask: do fitted values track the data? Is RMS small in context? Blindly quoting \(\hat{x}\) is not enough.
Positive semidefinite / definite (Boyd / class notes). A symmetric matrix \(P\) is positive semidefinite (PSD) if \(x^{\mathsf{T}}Px\ge 0\) for all \(x\); positive definite (PD) if \(x^{\mathsf{T}}Px>0\) for all \(x\neq 0\).
For any \(A\): \[
x^{\mathsf{T}}(A^{\mathsf{T}}A)x = \lVert Ax\rVert^2 \ge 0,
\] so \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\). It is positive definite precisely when \(Ax=0\Rightarrow x=0\), i.e. when \(A\) has \(\underline{\hspace{2.8cm}}\) columns — then the normal equations have a unique solution.

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Worked in class
W1. Tiny fit by hand / software. Four campus shuttle wait times (minutes) at hours \(t=1,2,3,4\) after 8am: \[
b=(6,\,7,\,10,\,11).
\] Model a line \(b\approx x_1 + x_2 t\) with \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1&1\\1&2\\1&3\\1&4
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Form \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) and \(A^{\mathsf{T}}b\) (or use A\b / lstsq).
Report \(\hat{x}=(x_1,x_2)\) and the fitted values \(\hat{b}=A\hat{x}\).
Compute \(r\) and RMS. In one sentence: is a linear trend reasonable here?

Expected (for checking): \(\hat{x}=(4,\,1.8)\) exactly from the normal equations; \(\hat{b}=(5.8,\,7.6,\,9.4,\,11.2)\); RMS \(=\sqrt{0.2}\approx 0.45\) minutes.
W2. Orthogonality. With your \(\hat{x}\) from W1, compute \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r\). Should it be near \((0,0)\)?
W3. Plot story. On axes “hour \(t\)” vs “wait (min)”, sketch data points and the fitted line. Where is the residual for \(t=1\) visible?
W4. PSD identity. Expand \(x^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}}Ax\) for \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}\) and a general \(x=(x_1,x_2)\). Confirm it equals \(\|Ax\|^2\) and is \(\ge 0\).
W5. PD vs PSD. Explain why \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) fails to be positive definite if the two columns of \(A\) are equal. What goes wrong for uniqueness of \(\hat{x}\)?

title: Lecture 39 — Least squares, data fitting, and positive definiteness
text:
Your turn
Y1. Using the W1 data, suppose software returns \(\hat{x}=(4,\,1.8)\). Compute \(\hat{b}_1=x_1+x_2\cdot 1\) and the first residual \(r_1=b_1-\hat{b}_1\).
Y2. True or false: \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always positive definite for every \(A\).
Y3. Why check \(A^{\mathsf{T}}r\approx 0\) after a least-squares solve?
Y4. A fit has RMS \(=0.02\) °C for outdoor temperature data that typically varies by \(10\) °C across the day. Useful model, or not? One sentence.






NoteAnswers (Your turn only)





Y1. \(\hat{b}_1=4+1.8=5.8\); \(r_1=6-5.8=0.2\).
Y2. False. \(A^{\mathsf{T}}A\) is always PSD, but PD only when \(A\) has linearly independent columns (equivalently \(\ker A=\{0\}\)).
Y3. It is the normal-equation / geometric check that the residual is orthogonal to \(C(A)\) — evidence that \(\hat{x}\) really is a least-squares critical point (up to roundoff).
Y4. Useful in context: RMS \(\ll\) the natural scale of the data, so typical pointwise error is tiny compared with day-scale variation.

title: Capstone — Low-rank frames vs differences
text:
The question
You get (or build) three grayscale frames \(F_1,F_2,F_3\), each an \(m\times n\) matrix of intensities.
Compare two encoding strategies with rank-\(k\) SVD approximations:







Plan
What you compress with a rank-\(k\) SVD




A — Independent frames
\(F_1\), \(F_2\), and \(F_3\) separately


B — Frame + differences
\(F_1\), then \(D_2=F_2-F_1\), then \(D_3=F_3-F_2\)



Driving question: For your data, when (if ever) is Plan B better than Plan A on accuracy, storage, and runtime / resource use — including the cost of computing the SVDs?
Computing an SVD is not free. Low-rank storage or faster later multiplies only help when the matrix is well approximated at modest \(k\) and you reuse the representation enough (or care enough about storage/transmission) to justify the factorization cost. Image examples are instructional.

When

title: Capstone — Low-rank frames vs differences
text:
What to turn in (Canvas)
One PDF (or short report + clearly labeled figures), individual submission, about 1–2 pages of writing plus figures/tables:

Data. Where the three frames came from (phone stills, course sample, synthetic frames, etc.) and size \(m\times n\).
Methods. Rank(s) \(k\) you tried; how you formed \(D_2,D_3\); how you rebuilt approximate frames under Plan B.
Evidence (required numbers).

Relative reconstruction error vs \(k\) for Plan A and Plan B (plot or table).
Storage count: full \(mn\) vs rank-\(k\) cost \(\approx k(m+n+1)\) per compressed matrix (and totals for A vs B).
Timing: at least one honest runtime comparison (e.g. SVD time vs applying a low-rank map, or Plan A vs B factorization time for the same \(k\)).

Conclusion. One clear recommendation: for your frames, prefer A, prefer B, or “depends,” with a quantitative reason and one limitation.

Gallery: 2–3 minute lightning talk or a station with one figure people can read in 30 seconds. Peers may ask about your numbers.

Success criteria (how it is graded, 25 points)








Criterion
Points
What “good” looks like

5

title: Capstone — Low-rank frames vs differences
text:
Technical notes
Storage (order of magnitude).

One full frame: \(mn\) numbers.
One rank-\(k\) factorization: about \(k(m+n+1)\) numbers (columns of \(U_k\), \(V_k\), and \(k\) singular values).
Plan A total (three frames): about \(3k(m+n+1)\).
Plan B total (three matrices): also about \(3k(m+n+1)\) at the same \(k\) — so Plan B wins on storage only if you can use a smaller \(k\) for differences while matching Plan A’s error, or if you choose different \(k\) per matrix on purpose.

Error. For a matrix \(A\) and approximation \(A_k\), a standard relative Frobenius error is \[
\frac{\lVert A-A_k\rVert_F}{\lVert A\rVert_F}.
\] Under Plan B, measure error on the reconstructed frames \(\widehat F_2=\widehat F_1+\widehat D_2\), etc., not only on the difference matrices.
Software sketch








Task
Octave
Python




SVD
[U,S,V] = svd(A)
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(A, full_matrices=False)


Rank-\(k\) rebuild
first \(k\) columns / \(\sigma\)’s
U[:,:k] @ np.diag(S[:k]) @ Vt[:k,:]


Frobenius norm
norm(A,'fro')
np.linalg.norm(A, 'fro')



Use grayscale (2D arrays). Color is optional enrichment only.

title: Quiz 8
text:
Core

Part A — Augmented matrix, eliminate, check
For each system: (i) write the augmented matrix \([A\mid b]\); (ii) solve by elimination (row operations on the augmented matrix); (iii) check by substituting your solution into the original equations (or computing \(Ax\) and comparing to \(b\)).
C8.1. (\(2\times 2\)) \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 + 2x_2 &= 5 \\
3x_1 - x_2 &= 1.
\end{aligned}
\]
C8.2. (\(3\times 2\) — three equations, two unknowns) \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 + x_2 &= 3 \\
2x_1 - x_2 &= 0 \\
3x_1 &= 3.
\end{aligned}
\]
C8.3. (\(2\times 3\) — two equations, three unknowns) \[
\begin{aligned}
x_1 + 2x_2 + x_3 &= 4 \\
2x_1 + 4x_2 + 2x_3 &= 8.
\end{aligned}
\] If there are infinitely many solutions, introduce a parameter \(t\) and write the general solution.


Part B — Name the elementary matrix
Use the templates at the end of the quiz (they will be provided). For each stated row operation on a system with the given number of equations, write the corresponding elementary matrix \(E\).
C8.4. Two equations: add \(-3\) times row 1 to row 2.
C8.5. Two equations: swap row 1 and row 2.
C8.6. Three equations: multiply row 2 by \(1/2\).
C8.7. Three equations: add \(2\) times row 1 to row 3.


Part C — Apply \(E\) and rewrite the system
C8.8. Let \[
[A\mid b]=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&|&3\\ 2&1&|&0\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
E=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ -2&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) Compute \(E\,[A\mid b]\) by hand.
(b) Rewrite the result as a system of equations.
C8.9. Let \[
[A\mid b]=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0&|&2\\ 0&1&1&|&3\\ 2&0&1&|&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
E=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ -2&0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) Compute \(E\,[A\mid b]\) by hand.
(b) Rewrite the result as a system of equations in \(x_1,x_2,x_3\).

title: Quiz 8
text:
Elementary-matrix templates (provided on the quiz)
Left-multiplying \([A\mid b]\) by \(E\) performs the row operation. Build \(E\) by doing that same operation to the identity.
Two equations (\(2\times 2\) templates):
Swap the two rows: \[
\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Multiply row 1 by \(c\neq 0\), or multiply row 2 by \(c\neq 0\): \[
\begin{bmatrix}c&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&c\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Add \(c\) times row 1 to row 2, or add \(c\) times row 2 to row 1: \[
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\c&1\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}1&c\\0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Three equations: start from \(I_3\) and edit the same spot. Examples:
Multiply row 2 by \(c\neq 0\): \[
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&c&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Add \(c\) times row 1 to row 3: \[
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\c&0&1\end{bmatrix}.
\]
(The extra number sits in the row you change, in the column of the row you copy from.)

text:

Fluency (complete prompts — practice these by hand)
C10.1. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\0&3\end{bmatrix}.
\] (a) Compute \(A^{-1}\) using the \(2\times 2\) formula (or by solving \(AB=I\)). (b) Check \(A^{-1}A=I\). (c) Solve \(Ax=(4,3)\) using \(x=A^{-1}b\).
C10.2. Decide whether each matrix is invertible. Give a one-line reason (dependent columns, \(Ax=0\), or \(\det\)).

\(\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\)

C10.3. True or false, with a one-line reason: for a single right-hand side \(b\), forming \(A^{-1}\) explicitly and then computing \(A^{-1}b\) is generally preferable to solving \(Ax=b\) with a solver / elimination.
C10.4. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 \\
2 & 4 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\] The RREF of \(A\) is \[
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 1 \\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{bmatrix}
\] (after row swaps / scaling as needed — use this RREF). Find \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\), a basis for \(C(A)\) using original columns, and a basis for \(N(A)\).
C10.5. Let \[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 \\
2 & 0 \\
0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\] Describe \(C(A)\) in words. Is \(b=(1,2,3)\) in \(C(A)\)? Find a basis for \(N(A)\) (or state that \(N(A)=\{0\}\)).
C10.6. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\) for an \(m\times n\) matrix with \(m\ge n\), then \(Ax=0\) has only the zero solution.
C10.7. Compute each determinant.

\(\det\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\det\begin{bmatrix}1&4&0\\0&-2&5\\0&0&3\end{bmatrix}\)
\(\det\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\4&2\end{bmatrix}\)

C10.8. Let \(A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-2\\1&0\end{bmatrix}\). Compute \(\det A\). Where do \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) go under \(x\mapsto Ax\)? What area does the unit square map to?
C10.9. True or false, with a one-line reason: if \(\det A=0\) for square \(A\), then \(A\) is not invertible and \(Ax=b\) fails to have a unique solution for every \(b\).
C10.10. Connect the ideas. For square \(A\), match each statement to the equivalent view (write the letter):


\(A\) is invertible


\(\operatorname{rank}(A)=n\) (full)


\(\det A\neq 0\)


\(N(A)=\{0\}\)


Which of (ii)–(iv) are equivalent to (i)?
C10.11 (cumulative, light). Let \(A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{bmatrix}\). What geometric map is \(x\mapsto Ax\)? Is \(A\) invertible? What is \(\det A\)?
